#5031. North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

Pyongyang has pushed back against the FBI’s attribution of the Binance attack, with Kim Yo Jong calling the US allegations politically motivated.

Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack and appeared to suggest, without evidence, that the US could have been behind the theft.

In a statement released via the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Tuesday, Kim rejected the FBI’s attribution of the attack to a North Korean-backed hacking group.

“The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” said Kim. “But the US assertion is an absurd rhetoric and nothing new.”

She described the allegations as a political provocation intended to damage North Korea’s international standing. The FBI also blamed North Korea for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, an accusation Kim also rejected on Tuesday.

“This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” said Kim.

Kim also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack.

“If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said.

The statement provided no evidence connecting Washington to the attack. Cointelegraph reached out to the FBI for comment.

Last week, blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs attributed the Binance attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor group with high confidence, citing onchain and offchain intelligence. Other investigators, including Chainalysis and ZachXBT, also linked the theft to North Korean hackers.

TRM Labs pointed to similarities with previous North Korean attacks, including advance preparation, the use of Tornado Cash to fund attacker wallets and the coordinated execution of previously obtained transaction signatures. However, it said the laundering activity differed from the pattern following the Bybit hack.

Onchain investigator ZachXBT also identified a connection between the Binance and Bitget hacks, saying stolen funds from both incidents were commingled at the same address after passing through THORChain. During early investigation into the hack, Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said preliminary findings linked IP addresses to VPN services used “by a certain DPRK group.”

Related: FBI blames North Korea for record $6.3B Binance hack

#5030. North Korea Denies $6.3B Binance Hack, Calls FBI Finding a 'Political Provocation'

North Korea Denies $6.3B Binance Hack, Calls FBI Finding a 'Political Provocation'

North Korea has rejected U.S. findings that it was behind the record hack of Binance, calling the FBI's attribution a "grave political provocation," Yonhap reported on Tuesday.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the U.S. misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," Kim Yo Jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said in a statement carried by the state-run Korean Central News Agency. She called the accusation a "sinister" attempt to damage North Korea's international image.

Kim also turned the blame back on Washington, pointing to the Trump administration's plan to use confiscated crypto as a strategic reserve. Anyone who looks at who will end up with "the so-called stolen cryptocurrency" once it is retrieved "may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident," she said.

The FBI said on Saturday that North Korean hackers it calls TraderTraitor were responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, confirming the attribution blockchain analytics firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis made last week. The FBI attributed the $1.5 billion hack of crypto exchange Bybit in February 2025 to the same group. North Korea has denied previous accusations of hacking.

The hackers are moving their haul quickly. North Korea is laundering the funds at a rate of roughly one new wallet every 25 seconds, across about 12,000 wallets, Decrypt reported on Monday. About $2.85 billion of the $6.43 billion stolen has been frozen or seized, compared with roughly 3% of the funds taken from Bybit.

Not all of the stolen funds are moving at the same pace. As of Monday, more than $1 billion in ETH and about $1.42 billion in BTC had seen limited onward movement, while other funds were moving rapidly across chains, blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis said. The activity so far is broadly consistent with the "immediate layering" phase seen after past North Korean hacks, though funds repeatedly returning to earlier addresses across thousands of transactions suggests automation, the firm said. It expects the scale of the theft to "strain the actors' trusted laundering channels," pushing funds toward bridges, instant exchanges and swapping services.

As of Nov 2, over $1B in ETH and ~$1.42 billion in BTC stolen from Binance have seen limited onward movement since the theft.

Other stolen funds are moving rapidly across chains.

These funds are not all progressing through the laundering process at the same pace. pic.twitter.com/ZEVCZzCDRM

— Chainalysis (@chainalysis) November 2, 2026

Binance did not respond to the BBC's questions about North Korea's alleged involvement. A company spokesperson told the outlet that a net $4.72 billion had been withdrawn since withdrawals resumed on Sunday, a "relatively limited portion" of total assets of about $157 billion.

By 10 p.m. ET on Monday, hourly deposits were exceeding withdrawals, "reflecting improving user activity and stabilizing flows," Binance tweeted. The exchange has since restored withdrawals for dozens more tokens on Ethereum and Solana.

Binance also said on Monday that users holding its 10 largest tokens, including BTC, ETH, USDT and USDC, can now verify that their balances are fully backed, using a zero-knowledge proof of its October 31 reserves snapshot. It has covered about 95% of the stolen assets, with the rest made up of less liquid tokens that take longer to buy, and plans to take a wider snapshot on Wednesday.

From Provence to the Côte d’Azur, the south of France offers a storybook mélange of rustic farmhouses, centuries-old castles and estates, along with honey-hued stone houses tucked into timeless hilltop towns.

Whether you fancy swimming in a pool besides your own château, late evening pétanque games at a centuries-old castle, gathering a group of friends at a hillside estate, or cozying up in a rustically romantic village apartment, Airbnb has options for turning every south of France fantasy into a reality. Tucked in the hilly countryside, proximity to both Alpine and Nordic skiing is the property’s main draw for those looking to hit the slopes. #5027. South Korea urges exchanges to boost cold storage after Binance hack

South Korean crypto exchanges are already required to hold at least 80% of customer crypto in cold wallets, but the regulator is urging more.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission has urged domestic crypto exchanges to increase the proportion of assets held in cold wallets after the $6.3 billion attack on Binance last week.

In a statement Monday, the FSC said it held an emergency meeting with the Financial Supervisory Service, the Financial Security Institute, the Digital Asset eXchange Alliance (DAXA) and major crypto service providers to review the impact of the Binance hack on South Korea’s crypto market and review exchanges’ security measures.

The FSC said it reviewed exchanges’ IT access controls, wallet withdrawal approval and signing procedures, and administrator privileges. It also urged providers to increase the proportion of assets held in offline cold wallets.

Attackers stole about $6.3 billion from Binance’s internet-connected hot wallets last week, moving most of the funds in about 20 minutes, according to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. Binance has said the vast majority of users’ assets are held in cold storage.

South Korean law already requires exchanges to hold at least 80% of users’ crypto assets in cold storage, though cold wallet holdings vary considerably among South Korea’s major exchanges.

At the end of September, Upbit’s cold wallet ratio stood at 99.17%, followed by Bithumb at 94.76% and Coinone at 85%, according to Financial Supervisory Service data cited by local media. Digital X, formerly Korbit, and GOPAX reported ratios of 82.79% and 80.54%, respectively.

Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

The FSC also urged providers to continuously monitor deposits and withdrawals, secure additional incident response personnel and promptly report and share information about unusual access attempts.

Operators were also asked to set aside additional reserves and implement other security measures that could be introduced immediately to prevent similar breaches. The regulator said it would continue working with relevant agencies and the industry to prevent further attacks and limit potential damage.

Cointelegraph reached out to Upbit, Bithumb, Coinone, Digital X and GOPAX for comment.

The FSC’s warning comes as the Bank of Korea separately surveys 18 banks and 13 brokerages about their exposure to crypto-related risks, including major exchange hacks and prolonged market downturns. The central bank’s review began before the Binance attack.

#5026. Liquid Network Restores Full Bitcoin Backing Two Months After $320M Exploit

Liquid Network Restores Full Bitcoin Backing Two Months After $320M Exploit

The Liquid Network's Bitcoin reserves have been fully restored, two months after self-described white-hat hackers drained most of them, the Liquid Federation said on Monday.

The federation said it had reestablished 1:1 Bitcoin backing for all LBTC, the token that represents Bitcoin on Liquid. The milestone follows the restoration of swaps between BTC and LBTC at a 1:1 rate through participating providers several weeks ago, it said.

The Liquid Federation is pleased to announce that the network’s bitcoin reserves have been fully restored, reestablishing 1:1 BTC backing for all LBTC.

This follows the restoration of BTC<>LBTC swaps several weeks ago, which have since allowed…

— Liquid Network 🌊 (@Liquid_BTC) November 3, 2026

Blockstream CEO Adam Back, whose company develops the technology behind Liquid, posted a screenshot of the network's dashboard showing assets matching liabilities at 100%, with a reserve deficit of 0.00 BTC. Users running their own Liquid nodes can verify the federation's reserves directly, the federation said.

It did not say how the shortfall left by the hack was covered.

Launched by Blockstream in 2018, Liquid is a Bitcoin sidechain, a separate blockchain that runs alongside Bitcoin, designed for faster and more private transfers. Users lock up BTC in a wallet controlled by the federation, a group of exchanges and other crypto companies that run the network, and receive the same amount of LBTC in return.

Asked on X what would stop a repeat of the hack, Back listed three hardened "lines of defense": refreshed peg-out authorization keys now held in cold hardware wallets, disabled proof validation caches along with a bug fix for nodes, and consensus rules that have been hardened to "fail closed." The network has also been through multiple third-party audits, he said.

"And lesson: treat with suspicion (don't trust, verify) AI suggested fixes," Back wrote.

Back had pointed to AI's growing role in security in an interview with Bloomberg Television on October 20, describing "a wave of AI-assisted security analysis" over the previous couple of months. "AI, of course, is a tool to help develop code and to secure the code, but also it can be used to find defects," he said, adding that it had been "affecting many companies in the sector." He said then that the hacked funds remained "under investigation."

The federation said it is modernizing Liquid's governance structure, introducing clearer responsibilities and oversight, and adding further technical and operational safeguards, with more details to come in the coming weeks.

On September 6, purported white-hat hackers withdrew about 4,000 BTC, then worth around $320 million, from Liquid's federation wallet, communicating with Blockstream through PGP-signed messages embedded in Bitcoin transactions.

The next day, they returned 3,400 BTC, worth about $269 million, after Blockstream said Liquid's bridge nodes had been patched, but kept roughly 598 BTC. Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet said that if the remaining coins were a negotiated reward, the arrangement looked "more like extortion than white-hat hacking."

Blockstream later refused to pay a ransom for the outstanding Bitcoin. "Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure," the company said. "It is not white-hat activity. It is theft."

#5024. Binance begins second withdrawal phase, exchange outflows slow

The exchange says additional assets will become available for withdrawal from 04:00 UTC on Tuesday as security checks are completed, following an initial reopening on Sunday.

Binance plans to begin a second phase of cryptocurrency withdrawals on Tuesday, as data shows withdrawal volumes have started to stabilize following last week’s $6.3 billion hack.

Withdrawals for additional assets are scheduled to resume progressively from 04:00 UTC on Tuesday, according to Binance’s latest recovery notice. The rollout follows an initial reopening on Nov. 1.

“Like phase one, reopening will roll out progressively across the assets as security and readiness checks are completed,” said Binance.

The exchange said it was prioritizing tokens based on user demand over the past week. Deposits remain available.

Networks part of the second phase of withdrawals include Binance Smart Chain, Ethereum, Solana, XRP Ledger, Sui, Arbitrum, Optimism, Tron and Base, according to Binance.

Binance’s list of assets planned for withdrawal. Source: Binance

On Monday, Binance said it also reopened withdrawals for several fiat currencies, including the US dollar, United Arab Emirates dirham, Vietnamese dong, Philippine peso and Indonesian rupiah, adding to a list of 23 other currencies already available for withdrawal.

Data from DefiLlama shows outflows from the crypto exchange have slowed since Sunday, with net outflows on Monday at $2.57 billion, compared to $6.1 billion the day before.

In a separate security reminder, Binance warned that scammers could exploit the phased reopening by impersonating the exchange and offering accelerated withdrawals, sell priority processing, help users claim compensation or direct them to move assets into a purported “Binance vault,” the exchange said.

“Anyone promising to expedite it for a fee is scamming you,” Binance said.

#5023. The Best Dining Room Lighting Ideas to Set Your Space Aglow

As romantic as candlelight dining sounds, it’s simply not practical (way too much wax!). The best dining room lighting ideas are thoughtfully planned: They take your actual eating habits, furniture proportions, room structure, and budget into consideration. They weigh the benefits of pendant lights vs. chandeliers vs. flush mounts and wall sconces, not to mention bulb type.

Lighting, it turns out, gets pretty involved—which is why we’ve tapped interior designers from around the country for their brightest ideas. And though the considerations are complex, modern lighting can be just as romantic as the candlelight option. “The evolving landscape is opening the door to more thoughtful layers and innovative ideas for how lighting can shape a space,” says Mike Shively of Chicago-based AD PRO firm En Masse Architecture and Design. “Lighting and coziness are both things we associate with luxury today, and neither necessarily comes down to price.”

In fashion designer Marysia Reeves’s Venice Beach home, a breezy, lantern-like fixture hovers above the wood dining table.

Pendant lighting gets more playful when each piece hangs at a different height. The look works especially well with a vaulted ceiling, as evidenced by this dining room set in a pavilion at the back of the house. “A cluster of glass pendants hung at staggered heights works alongside a pair of table lamps on the sideboard to create warm, layered light,” says Lucas Goldbach of En Masse Architecture and Design, who worked on the project.

The varying heights of the pendants gives this light fixture some dimension.

In this stunner of an LA home by design collective the Archers, a Le Corbusier–inspired table is lit with simple can overhead lights (definitely dimmable versions).

Lighting options are about more than just form. A more traditional shape can look entirely new when cast in a surprising material. “Our recommendation is to rethink conventional finishes and materials wherever possible,” says Sarah Goesling of Goesling Group, an AD PRO Directory firm based in Chicago. “For a chain-mail fixture, look beyond stainless steel to a striking yellow gold. For braided metal hardware, trade the ruggedness of wrought iron for the refined sheen of polished gunmetal.”

For a dining room in a midcentury-modern home, Goesling Group chose an appropriately retro 1950s-inspired Nabila chandelier by Tooy. And to add a modernized touch through the materials, they went with smoked glass around the bulbs.

A Sputnik-style fixture draws the eye up in this dining room by Goesling Group.

If you find an antique fixture you love, it might be worth rewiring the piece. Source on sites like eBay, Etsy, and 1stdibs, or take a lap around your local flea market. Alternatively, scour relatives’ attics and basements for a fixture with some family history. In the dining room below, designed by En Masse Architecture and Design, the light fixture was originally bought by the homeowner’s parents and was refurbished by Archistoric. “It became the inspiration for many of the metal finishes used throughout the new design,” says Goldbach.

This En Masse Architecture and Design dining space is crowned by an heirloom chandelier, refurbished by Archistoric.

Sconces, floor lamps, even table lamps can do the job of overhead pendant and flush-mount fixtures—so don’t force one if you’re not sure you like the look at all (proof, via Amélie Colombet’s apartment).

Fixtures made from natural alabaster stone are popular because of the warm, glare-free glow they emit. And because the translucent material has natural veining, no two pieces are alike. You can find alabaster in a variety of shapes—including linear forms, mini pendants, and semi-flush-mount ceiling lights—and while it’s generally pretty pricey (ranging anywhere from $300 for a single alabaster pendant lamp to $3,000 for a row of pendants), it’s also a durable material that lasts.

In the dining nook below, designed by Goesling Group, the minimal fixture makes a major impression. “It’s a solid alabaster stone piece lit all the way around the rim that looks like the moon when it glows,” says Goesling.

The pendant sets a striking tone in this cozy dining nook by Goesling Group.

If you have no interest in hardwiring a thing . . .Get an arc floor lampYou can have proper overhead lighting for your dining area without hardwiring a thing overhead. All you need is an arc floor lamp; they plug right into a wall outlet but stand tall, with a long, curved neck that will position the bulb and shade directly over your table. (How’s that for simplified?) The Arco floor lamp by Flos is a classic, but more budget-conscious shoppers can spring for similar styles from retailers like Wayfair (or even Amazon!).

If you’re trying to decide between options . . .Take the shape and style of your table into considerationThe overhead fixture you choose and the table itself “don’t have to [have] a direct geometrical correlation, but there should be some proportional consideration,” says Russell Groves of New York City–based Groves & Co. A long or unusually large chandelier would obviously overpower a short table, and vice versa: A teeny-tiny bulb might look silly above a big table. Same goes for the look: A lovely old farmhouse table would do well with a lovely farmhouse fixture or something super-modern for contrast—but either way, they should be considered together.

If you’d like to jazz up a fixture you already own . . .Customize the lampshadeA reflective material inside the shade will help cast light back down toward the table, Groves points out, while perforated shades will turn any bulb into a twinkly light (if that’s your prerogative). “Textured fabrics like raw silk will add a beautiful warmth and shadow to a room,” he says, but should you require a more directional cast, “an opaque shade wouldn’t give you a lot of glow in the room but would put more on the table.” Just because a fixture has shades you’re not into doesn’t mean it’s the end of the line. Swap them out!

If you’re sick of the typical dining room look . . .Consider less-traditional fixtures“Unreal times call for surreal styles, and lighting is emerging as a particularly compelling canvas for experimentation,” says Goesling. “From blown-glass designs with off-kilter stripes, to chain-mail, tapestry, and wrought iron reimagined through unexpected finishes and geometric patterns, these materials and techniques are taking on a new life. We anticipate seeing this influence extend across lighting, from woven metal sheaths and illustrative shades to sculptural, cast forms.”

A unique accent light sometimes even doubles as art. Such is the case in a Chicago penthouse designed by Kuchar, which features a dining room fixture with a strikingly sinuous form. “Going for the cool, funky light fixture has become the new normal among our residential clients,” says Sarah Kuchar-Parkinson, owner and creative director of the Chicago-based studio. “Not only does it bring brightness and light, but it adds architectural interest and an element of quirk.”

A statement-making light fixture hovers above the dining room table of this Kuchar-designed Chicago penthouse.

When hanging a pendant or a chandelier . . .Take care to hang it at the correct heightToo high and a pendant lamp might look stuck to the ceiling, constricted; too low and you won’t be able to see your guests around it. Somewhere in between is just right, so step back and consider it at various lengths before settling on one. “When you’re seated, you don’t want [the fixture] to be in your face—the same way everyone gets annoyed when flowers are in the way,” Groves says.

If you’re into geometric lines . . .Get creative with the cordWhen hanging a pendant lamp with a very simple silhouette, feel free to get creative with the cord: Zigzag it from wall to wall around a corner, tack it in swags along the ceiling, or loop it over a hook on the wall.

To soften overly bright overheads . . .Add a dimmerDesigner Sam Allen of Sam Allen Interiors, based in Weston, Connecticut, feels strongly about the worth of a dimmer switch: “If your dining room chandelier is not hooked up to a dimmer, call an electrician right now. I mean it. Don’t even finish reading this—call your electrician first.” With the simple pressing of a lever or turning of a knob, dimmable lighting allows you to control the brightness of the bulbs, which is particularly important if you’re dealing with often-harsh overhead lighting. “To me, chandeliers should mimic candlelight,” says Groves—and that warm, dim glow is possible if you just install dimmers. Plus, they’re available in both modern and traditional silhouettes that will add considerably more charm to the walls than those plastic switch plates you hate anyway.

To make the room multifunctional . . .Supplement the lighting solution you chooseIf you end up setting your table with some nice, warm candlelight, you might need to add sconces or downlights to supplement that glow when the room is used for anything other than an intimate dinner. (Dining room tables are very good for DIY projects, we’d like to note.) And to up a room’s cozy factor, lean into lamps. “The more lamps the better,” says Goldbach. “We like using smaller-scale lamps and vintage pieces in unexpected ways to create a warm, layered atmosphere. Multiple light sources can make the space feel cozier and more inviting, especially as the days get shorter.”

If you’re a fanatic about light quality . . .Be selective with the bulbsWarm white light, cool light, bright light—you can get exactly the brightness level you desire with the right bulb. For lots of ambience, try vintage-inspired filament bulbs. If it’s more of a particular shape and style you’re after for an exposed-bulb fixture, try decorative bulbs. And for the ultimate in energy efficiency, invest in LED bulbs, which are up to 90 percent more efficient than traditional light bulbs.

#5022. What Is The Bare Minimum Amount Of Strength Training You Need To Do For It To Be Effective? Here's What Trainers Say

Right up there with a balanced diet, strength training is the OG biohack for longevity, and the key to a strong, healthy body. But whether you’re a beginner or seasoned athlete, that begs the question: How much strength training do you actually need to see results?

If you look to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for answers, they say that adults need at least two days of “muscle-strengthening activity" per week for their overall health. But, resistance training even once a week was enough to make progress for beginners, per a study in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation.

"While it may seem the small amount of volume would be insignificant, this study demonstrates that some exercise is better than no exercise,” says certified personal trainer Natalya Vasquez. But as your skill level progresses, you’ll need to increase the intensity and volume of your workouts to elicit more muscle growth.

Below, experts explain exactly how much strength training is enough based on your fitness level and goals.

Meet the experts: Tina Tang, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, strength coach, and founder of Iron Strong Fitness. Natalya Vasquez, CPT, is a certified personal trainer, health coach, and founder of On Your Terms Coaching.

The following cheat-sheet will give you an idea of how many days a week you should strength train.

While once a week was enough for the folks in the aforementioned study to make progress, they only looked at a single exercise: the leg press. Vasquez says that ideally, beginners looking to build total-body muscle and strength should start with two, or even three, nonconsecutive strength training sessions per week.

This frequency helps build a habit (key for those just starting out) and provides your body with the necessary stimulus for initial muscle growth, while also allowing for plenty of time to recover. But, your sessions don't have to be long: Initially, each session can be as short as 15 to 20 minutes, and you can gradually increase to 45- to 60-minute workouts as you build endurance, says certified personal trainer Tina Tang, CPT.

As for how you structure your workouts, Vasquez says you can either do two to three full-body workouts, or a three-day split, like a push/pull/legs workout, where your training is organized by muscle group.

For a full-body routine, Vasquez suggests completing one exercise per muscle group for three to five sets of five to eight reps per workout. For a three-day split, complete three to four exercises for the same muscle group for two to three sets of five to eight reps.

Vasquez likes the five to eight rep range because she says this helps develop functional hypertrophy: “We don’t just want to gain muscle, we want to have actual strength where this muscle growth is functional,” she says.

“You don’t need complicated gym equipment to get results,” says Vasquez. “Dumbbells and bands are affordable, convenient, and versatile options for exercising at home, and as your strength increases, gym access may be beneficial since it’ll give you additional equipment and a wider selection of weights.”

In this case, the trainers suggest strength training three times a week, and depending on the intensity and volume of the workout, each session should range between 30 to 60 minutes, Tang says. “This frequency is effective for preserving muscle mass and strength while ensuring adequate recovery and adaptation.”

However, overall volume may be more important that days per week, according to a 2021 review in Sports Medicine. The researchers conclude that it's possible to see gains by training anywhere from one to four days per week so long as you're getting in at least four sets of six to 15 reps per muscle group per week.

The key here will be to follow the principle of progressive overload. Gradually increasing the weight, sets and or reps, over time will continually challenge the muscles, stimulate growth, and improve bone density, says Tang. “The body craves movement, and once it's accustomed to a certain level of activity, it needs more of a challenge to keep making gains."

Good news: The longer you’ve been strength training, the less work you’ll need to maintain your gains since your muscles are composed of more fibers, says Vasquez. “So if you’ve been strength training five times per week for a decade and then something happens in your life that doesn’t allow you to work out as much, you’ll still be able to maintain your muscle with one full-body workout per week,” she says. However, this would be the bare minimum, and resistance training two to three times a week is still the ideal sweet spot.

In terms of the type of training, Tang also recommends full-body workouts to maintain balanced muscle development and overall strength. Look to hit all the major movement patterns for best results. For each exercise, Vasquez says to aim to complete three to five sets of five to eight reps.

Aside from logging miles, strength training at least twice a week is a crucial part of every running regimen, says Tang. “Ideally, one session can focus on bilateral, foundational movements, while a second session allows for a more specialized approach, targeting unilateral exercises, core stability, and hip strength,” she explains. “This balance ensures you're not only building overall strength but also addressing the specific needs that support running performance and injury prevention.”

Indeed, the addition of two to four strength training sessions a week helped mid- to long-distance runners prevent injury and run faster, according to a 2024 meta-analysis in the journal Sports Medicine.

Workouts should range between 30 to 60 minutes and rep ranges can vary from five to eight (with heavier weight and for more advanced strength trainers) to 12 to 20 reps (for runners newer to strength training and using lighter weights), Vasquez says.

FWIW, the meta-analysis notes that plyometric training and "high load" strength training (using weights at 80% of your one rep max or heavier), specifically, improved running economy.

For this goal, Tang says to strength train at least twice a week. Doing so "helps build and maintain muscle mass and bone density, which is crucial for protecting bones and joints as we age, and this frequency provides a balance between stimulating the muscles and allowing for adequate recovery,” she says.

Plus, regular resistance training helps strengthen tendons and ligaments, in turn, supporting joint stability and overall musculoskeletal health, she adds.

Full-body workouts and compound exercises like deadlifts, overhead presses, and squats are ideal since they involve multiple joints and mimic how your body moves in real life, says Vasquez. Depending on your experience, this could look like choosing two to three exercises and doing three to five sets for five to eight reps (to focus on building functional strength) per workout.

No matter your goals, strength training is certainly worth your time. Aside from supporting your overall wellbeing, picking up weights can prevent injury, improve metabolic health, reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease, and support bone density, especially in women, says Vasquez.

In fact, approximately one in five women over age 50 have osteoporosis (a condition that causes bones to become weak and brittle), but strength training can help enhance bone density and reduce the risk of fractures, says Tang.

Sarcopenia, an age-related progressive loss of muscle mass strength, is another common condition among women, and after age 30, you can gradually begin losing muscle mass each decade. Fortunately, strength training can again help combat the effects and reverse muscle loss, says Tang.

Finally, regular weight training supports balance, mobility, and functional strength which are crucial for performing daily activities and living independently, Tang says. “Strength training acts as an investment in our future health, ensuring that we maintain physical strength and resilience for the long term.”

Andi Breitowich is a freelance writer who covers health, fitness, relationships, beauty, and smart living. She is a graduate of Emory University and Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism. Her work has appeared in Women's Health, POPSUGAR, Food & Wine, What To Expect, Cosmopolitan, Men's Health, and elsewhere. As a former collegiate pole vaulter, she loves all things fitness and has yet to meet a group workout class she doesn't like.

#5020. Binance Misses Monthly Luna Classic Burn for First Time Since 2023

Binance Misses Monthly Luna Classic Burn for First Time Since 2023

Centralized exchange Binance has burned Luna Classic tokens on the first of every month since 2023, when Do Kwon's Terra Luna empire came crumbling down. At the start of November, however, that burn has not occurred.

Luna Classic (LUNC) is the original native token for the Terra blockchain, which Terraform Labs founder Do Kwon forked and left behind in 2022 in a bid to rescue his collapsing project. Kwon was later convicted of fraud and sentenced to 15 years in prison for his role in Terra’s $40 billion implosion. Yet the decentralized network he left behind has kept running, propped up by a passionate community of supporters who have sunk time, effort and money into keeping it alive.

Binance started the burns after Terra Classic’s community voted to burn a portion of every on-chain LUNC transaction in late 2022, with the exchange pledging to burn half of the trading fees earned from the token. In practice, this has come in the form of a batch of burns happening at the start of every month since March 2023, but, according to StatsBin data, November's burn has yet to come in.

Some Luna Classic investors are concerned about Binance's lack of monthly burn, while others point to last week's record-breaking hack of the exchange as a reason behind the burn's delay.

"It is an important sign of support and a vital part of the overall burn campaign," Dawid Skinder, brand and user experience ecosystem contributor for Terra Classic, told Decrypt. "It might be that it is just an operational issue after the biggest hack ever. Hopefully that is the case, Terra Classic does not need another problem."

Binance was hacked for $6.3 billion on Friday, which the FBI has attributed to TraderTraitor—the North Korean group blamed for the Bybit hack. It has been labelled the biggest crypto hack in history, with estimated losses at four times the previous record of $1.5 billion from the Bybit heist.

The exchange has been reopening withdrawals on the platform in stages, with the latest taking place late on Monday for dozens of Ethereum and Solana tokens. Some investors have questioned whether the LUNC burn is a priority for the exchange as it attempts to recover from the hack.

— Tango and Cash (@ThisDud30190229) November 2, 2026

"Yes, the hack was a problem," prominent Luna Classic community member Pedro, better known as Vegas, told Decrypt. "At the moment, we are helping them to keep LUNC and LUNA safe."

He has long claimed to be in direct contact with Binance regarding LUNC issues, though this has yet to be verified. Vegas claims Binance is working on security maintenance after the hack and is moving LUNC to a more secure wallet before proceeding with the burn.

Binance did not respond to Decrypt's request for comment.

The exchange has paused its LUNC burns once before, withholding contributions at the end of 2022 after the Terra Classic community voted to re-mint burned tokens as a development fund. Binance halved its burn to 50% of trading fees and only resumed in March 2023, once the community had scrapped the re-mints.

Luna Classic has dropped 7.9% in value over the past week to $0.0000417, per Decrypt data, and is down 99.99% from its all-time high of $119.18. Investors believe the Binance burn being paused is just one of many issues the token faces.

Skinder told Decrypt that Luna Classic needs to fix its lack of products, improve its marketing, conduct a proper audit, and protect itself against quantum attacks. Skinder said he believes in a revival but claims that it is difficult with decentralized governance and "amateur validators."

So, why bother? Why not spend time on another chain?

"There are X number of chains in a better state than Terra Classic. None of them (except Bitcoin, probably) have that history and narrative (biggest crypto revival ever). None of them have 20+ stablecoins that are waiting to be re-pegged and restored," Skinder said. "Low chance of success, big upside if done. Great history to be part of."

#5019. 12 Best Historic Hotels and Airbnbs That Feel Like Time Traveling (2026)

There are plenty of impressive stays out there, no matter your destination of choice. But booking a historic hotel or Airbnb rental with a storied past—tales of tenants, centuries-old architecture, or whatever else might land a property on a local registrar—is the difference between a simple spot to snooze at night and your next dinner party conversation. From former artists’ homes and firehouses to castles and celebrity-studded hotels, we’ve curated several beguiling places around the world to lay your head at night. As is the case with older buildings, some require a bit of flexibility—say, an outdoor shower or a less-than-fully-equipped kitchen—while others offer a portal to the past (some spots on this list predate the 16th century) rich with amenities and luxury.

The following historical hotels and homes have a story to tell, and guests get a front-row seat.

Perks: Shared beach access, in-unit washer and dryer, sound system, indoor fireplace, fire pit

Architect Frank Lloyd Wright built a lot of incredible spaces for others, but this is the very one he contributed to a Life Magazine article back in 1938 as part of a feature about dream homes. The four-bedroom estate is full of windows (the 63-foot living room has an entire wall of them), and each space is bursting with midcentury furniture and decor. Walking into each room feels like unlocking a new level of a time capsule, from the shag-carpeted primary bedroom to the brick-walled kitchen. While spring, summer, and fall are beautiful times to visit Wisconsin, the fire pit (and hammock) outside is still inviting come winter and snow. From $841 per night.

Perks: Badminton net, steam room, gym, BBQ grill, EV charger

This is the perfect pit stop on a road trip through the Highlands. Hidden in the depths of a former abbey, this one-bedroom space used to be the “writing room” for the monastery. The bed is surrounded by stained glass windows, which look out over the gardens and Loch Ness (yes, of Nessie fame). Guests have access to the neighboring Highland Club, which houses an incredible indoor pool, sauna, tennis court, and so much more. While the kitchen and appliances are newer additions, you will find pieces of furniture from the original space peppered throughout the rental (a wooden bench here, a tapestry there). From $468 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, patio, free parking, pool, outdoor shower

If daydreams of your next trip are filled with al fresco dinners, this two-bedroom home will do you one better by adding bird’s-eye ocean vistas to the scene. Once a windmill that used to grind wheat for flour production, it now houses an outdoor kitchen, a bedroom with a view, and an outdoor shower. The scenes from the top bedroom are really something to write home about—wake up to mountain views and the ocean beyond. The pool is the best spot to take in the sunset before retreating to the open-air dining space for good eats and conversation. From $224 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, Wi-Fi, luggage drop-off, radiant heating, fireplace

This historic Airbnb is known as La Romantica, which should tell you all you need to know. The one-bedroom rental can be found in the oldest section of the property (which dates back earlier than the 1400s), there’s a private entrance, ancient stone walls, antique Italian furniture, and a fireplace that’s perfect for fighting off a chilly night. This is a spot where you do a bit of time traveling, both indoors and out when you decide to explore the surrounding UNESCO heritage town, Teggiano, which is known for its museums (the Diocesan Museum, Herb Museum, and Museum of Folk Traditions, to name a few) and its 13 churches. Guests at this one-bedroom stay are located right in the middle of town and within walking distance of everything you’d need, so slipping out for a quick dinner, coffee at one of the cafes, or a sunset stroll along medieval architecture is always on the itinerary. From $154 per night.

Perks: Pet friendly, air conditioning, private parking available, fireplace, historic decor

Built in 1884, this was Washington, DC’s first fully African American fire company and the set of a Netflix show: Check out Stay Here, season one, episode eight. Located in the Shaw neighborhood, a historic district, there are plays to attend (Howard Theatre), drinks to be had (Blagden Alley), and music to take in (Eighth Street Lounge and Bar). The five-bedroom rental even has the original fire pole and you can see previous tenants in the photography that decorates the walls. From $860 per night.

Perks: Shared beach access, sound system, exercise equipment, fire pit

Step right into the world of painter Reginald Marsh when you stay at this two-bedroom getaway with forest views. A pond anchors one side of the property, and the expansive lawns are landscaped with long, post-dinner strolls in mind. As secluded as it feels, it’s a short walk to the center of Woodstock and all of its restaurants, bars, cafes, and shops. And while you’re not near any national parks, the home’s private waterfall (you read that correctly) borders a public preserve that’s open for exploring. The library inside will pull you back indoors, though, as will the wood-burning stove on chilly nights. The outdoor dining space is great for summertime grilling, but the full kitchen indoors is a delight to work in. From $619 per night.

Perks: Central location, trendy bars and restaurant, 24-hour fitness center, balcony access, Aqua di Parma and Byredo toiletries

Centrally located in Madrid’s Plaza de las Cortes, the historic Palace Hotel reopened its doors in 2025 to unveil property-wide updates—including its main lobby, dining accommodations, and 470 rooms—the result of a two-year renovation project with reimagined interiors by designer Lázaro Rosa-Violán. Dating back to 1912, The Palace has seen notable guests like Salvador Dalí and Ernest Hemingway, and is even credited as the first hotel in the country to have private toilets in its quarters.

Today, guests can appreciate pieces of the property’s historic past through a modern lens. Surrounded by bespoke fixtures custom designed by Rosa-Violán, vintage tapestries hang with contemporary Joan Miro prints in La Cúpula Restaurant. Inside the inviting suites, updated bathrooms feature original red marble stone reminiscent of Paloma Elsesser’s luxurious tub. Just a five-minute walk away, art aficionados can spend long hours wandering through the Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum and the Prado museum, or take a stroll through El Retiro Park. “The hotel staff at The Palace are some of the friendliest I’ve encountered,” says commerce editor Audrey Lee. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu. If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” From $1,060 per night.

Perks: Spa, fitness center, concierge, Smart TVs, room service

The history of the Waldorf Astoria runs deep. Originally designed in 1893 as two side-by-side hotels built by feuding family members, the collective property was demolished in 1929 to make room for the Empire State Building’s construction. It was reopened in its current Park Avenue location in 1931, breaking records as the largest and tallest hotel in the world (at the time). Its Art Deco architecture and interiors caught the eyes of royals, celebrities, and politicians around the world. The guest book includes names such as Nikola Tesla, Winston Churchill, Zsa Zsa Gabor, the Obamas, and so many more. After being closed for extensive renovations, the property is planning a grand re-opening for Spring 2025. From $1,221 per night.

Perks: Irene Forte spa, indoor lap pool, three on-site restaurants, whisky tasting experience, afternoon tea, views of Edinburgh landmarks

A historic landmark, the Balmoral is widely recognized for its 190-foot clock tower—famously set three minutes fast, except on New Year’s Eve—that has been part of the Edinburgh skyline since opening in the early 1900s. J.K. Rowling even finished the final Harry Potter book on January 11, 2007, in Suite 552—now commemorated with an owl door knocker and an in-room bust of the Greek god Hermes that Rowling signed. “The Balmoral does rest and relaxation like no other through comforting amenities, charming interiors, and hearty cuisine,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “After a long day of taking in Edinburgh’s historic sights, there was nothing I looked forward to more than the treats from turndown service and a long soak in the glossy marble tub.” Guests also return for the sprawling bedrooms, some of which frame picturesque views of Edinburgh Castle. The stays showcase cozy design with contemporary wallpaper prints, surprisingly neutral plaid furniture, and ultrasoft wool bed covers. From $399 per night.

Perks: Presidential, royal, and celebrity clientele; iconic Bemelmans Bar; walking distance to Central Park

Nestled on 76th Street off Madison Avenue, the Carlyle first opened its doors in 1930. Since then, presidents, royalty, and movie stars have all sought refuge in the hallowed hotel. “You can have breakfast next to Daniel Patrick Moynihan or Tom Ford,” Los Angeles–based designer and AD100 Hall of Famer Michael S. Smith once described. “It's like a big hotel in a small town, the grande dame of New York.” The interiors blend Art Deco touches and New York eclecticism with classic architecture through a layered mix of vintage-inspired furniture silhouettes, contemporary art, and splashy chandeliers. One of the hotel’s top attractions for locals and hotel guests alike is the iconic Bemelmans Bar, outfitted with whimsical wall murals by Madeline author and illustrator Ludwig Bemelmans. The classic martini is a failsafe order, though you could go for the namesake Madeline's Vesper or Bobby’s Manhattan (an homage to cabaret singer Bobby Short, a longtime fixture of Café Carlyle, another classic destination within the Carlyle). From $1,323 per night.

Celebrating its 100th birthday this year, Hotel Figueroa was founded in partnership with The Young Women's Christian Association (YWCA) as a safe haven for solo female travelers. The Downtown Los Angeles fixture was the first property that allowed unaccompanied women to check in without a male chaperone—something most hotels prohibited at the time. Today, Spanish Revival design influences flourish in the space: Expect curated art (exclusively by female artists), sophisticated tilework, and modern furnishings. As you dip in the coffin-shaped pool straight from the 1920s while surrounded by 50-year-old cacti, enjoy craft cocktails and bites from the poolside bar, La Casita. For a more substantial meal, the restaurant-in-residence Florence by the Water serves up Italian classics. From $229 per night.

Perks: Proximity to landmarks, celebrity guest roster, traditional afternoon tea, live music, private tours and experiences available upon request

Widely recognized as London’s oldest luxury hotel, updates like glossy marble bathrooms, vibrant textiles, and mahogany walk-in closets have breathed new life into the historic stay. At the same time, homages to the original architecture—in stained-glass windows, untouched entryways, and wrought-iron façade detailing—forge bonds to its heritage. “You might think the main attraction of Brown’s is its proximity to landmarks like Buckingham Palace and Hyde Park, but it’s actually the inviting staff and dapper design that make this stay more like a home than a stopover,” says Lee. Past literary guests of note include Rudyard Kipling, Bram Stoker, Agatha Christie, and Stephen King; King even outlined his bestseller Misery during one of his stays. Situated in the upscale Mayfair neighborhood, world-class shopping and top London museums ensure your agenda stays full. From $966 per night.

Craving an escape? From colorful carry-ons to cleverly designed packing cubes (how did we ever travel without them?), shop everything you need to make the journey in style—and as streamlined and stress-free as possible.

#5018. UK warns AI ransomware attack on infrastructure ‘highly likely’ by 2028

The warning comes as UK cyber officials also flag growing threats from state-backed hackers targeting government officials and politicians.

AI-powered malware is highly likely to be used in a ransomware attack targeting UK critical national infrastructure by 2028, the country’s National Cyber Security Centre has warned.

The assessment, published in the NCSC’s Annual Review 2026, says artificial intelligence will increase the scale and efficiency of ransomware operations, social engineering and vulnerability exploitation.

“It is also highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” the report states.

The warning forms part of a broader assessment linking cyber threats to the UK’s economic and national security. The NCSC also warned China, Russia and other nation-states will use “AI cyber” to achieve their geopolitical goals, increasing the scale and speed of cyber threats facing the UK.

Beyond ransomware, the NCSC highlighted the growing threat of state-backed cyber espionage targeting politicians, government officials and other high-risk individuals.

During the year, the NCSC observed persistent spear‑phishing activity against high‑risk individuals and increasing efforts to compromise messaging applications.

In March, Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian state hackers were targeting officials, military personnel and civil servants worldwide. Attackers impersonated Signal support to hijack accounts.

“Technology has always influenced cyber security. What is different today is the pace. The ability of state actors to harness new technologies will increasingly determine their effectiveness,” said the NCSC.

#5016. I’m a Doctor and I Won’t Touch Honey Packs. Here’s What I Do Before Sex Instead

Ahead, three tried-and-true strategies for better, longer-lasting erections.

IF YOU HAVE difficulty getting erections or simply want to spruce up your sex life, chances are you’ve heard about honey packs. The sachets of the sweet stuff are all over social media, promising enhanced sexual performance through stronger, long-lasting erections.

At first glance, you might find this a “natural” alternative for young guys who don’t want pills or painful-sounding ED procedures like shock wave therapy. After all, the packets do feature pictures of honey and bees swarming on honeycombs, and honey is usually one of the first ingredients—a food many dudes already drizzle in oatmeal and tea. What could go wrong?

MH did a deep dive last year into whether honey packs actually work. The TL;DR version is that despite the alluring promise of near-instant, rock-hard erections, you’re really taking a gamble on what you’re putting in your body. Natural ingredients like honey and ginseng provide a “trivial” performance-enhancing effect and multiple honey pack supplement companies have been flagged by the FDA for having hidden and unknown dosages of ingredients not included in the label, like tadalafil (the active ingredient in Cialis), sildenafil (the active ingredient in Viagra), and acetaminophen.

That’s why doctors have big safety concerns about honey packs, says Scott Miller, MD, a urologist and director of robotic surgery at Wellstar Health System. “If they can’t tell me what’s in them, then it’s an absolute no.” So if honey packs are out, what are some ways to help you get hard and stay hard? We turned to the experts, asking urologists what they do to prepare in lieu of popping a pack.

HONEY PACKS (AND even gas station dick pills) aren’t worth your time or money. But not all supplements need to be ruled out, says Philip Werthman, MD, a urologist and director of the Center for Male Reproductive Medicine and Vasectomy Reversal. For guys with mild ED or who just want to optimize their libido, he recommends L-arginine supplements.

L-arginine is an amino acid that supports blood flow through nitric oxide production. Nitric oxide allows blood vessels to open fully and allow more blood flow to come into the penis.

“The penis is a hemodynamic organ. It works on blood flow. There has to be stimulation and a relationship that is functional between the nerves and the blood vessels,” says Dr. Werthman. “Anything that helps nitric oxide stick around longer will cause more blood flow to come in and maybe give a better quality erection.”

If possible, he recommends choosing L-arginine supplements containing L-citrulline (a precursor to L-arginine) or pycnogenol. The latter is an antioxidant made from the bark of a tree and is a powerful antioxidant used often in the fertility world, says Dr. Werthman. In concert with L-arginine, the combo helps to boost erections.

There is one caveat. For the effects to really work, you need to take this supplement on a daily basis. A single scoop the night before a sexual encounter won’t make much of a difference.

“It’s the kind of thing you put into your supplement stack,” says Dr. Werthman. Beyond healthy erections, nitric oxide helps with increasing blood flow all over the body, potentially providing extra benefits to your brain, heart, and muscles if you’re working out.

Buyer Beware: Supplements are not FDA-regulated, and some can get sketchy. Consider getting a product tested and certified by a third-party testing facility to verify the supplement’s safety and quality.

OYSTERS AND CHAMPAGNE get a lot of hype as aphrodisiacs. But Dr. Werthman says the true value is eating foods high in L-arginine. Here are some examples:

Additionally, watermelon is one of the best foods to eat on the day you’re having sex because of its high citrulline content, says Dr. Werthman. So, while spontaneous sex is great, scheduling sex can help you fuel your body (and boner) accordingly.

As for what’s on the don’t eat list? Nothing, but both urologists say it’s best to avoid alcohol before sex. You might gain a little liquid courage, but the buzz kills erections. Alcohol slows down brain signals related to arousal and decreases the ability of blood vessels to trap blood in the penis.

CORTISOL, ALSO KNOWN as your body’s stress hormone, is one of the biggest killers of testosterone and erections. When your body is in fight-or-flight mode, Dr. Werthman says, the last thing it’s thinking about is having sex.

The trademarks of a stressful lifestyle—lack of sleep, long working hours, and a poor diet—can all create barriers to intimacy, says Dr. Miller. Setting aside time to take care of yourself physically will help with performing at your best.

For example, a meditation session or some light stretching can relieve some stress temporarily. You also might want to consider a quick workout. Now, Dr. Werthman warns that a single sweat session won’t do much for your penile health (over time, consistent exercise does support blood flow and cardiovascular health, helping you last longer). But in terms of mental health, the stress-relieving benefits of pushups or a quick jog can help you get amped for the main event. Plus, the endorphins in your body can shake off any pre-sex nerves and make you feel more confident in your body. One study involving over 128,000 people found all types of physical activity—walking, resistance training, Pilates, and yoga—effective in improving anxiety symptoms.

Granted, for some people, sex itself is the stress reliever. But if you tense up thinking about the actual act, Dr. Werthman advises taking it slow. Get out of your head and focus on increasing erotic arousal through kissing and other forms of foreplay, then seeing if you want to go further. “It’s about being comfortable with your partner,” he says. “You want a dynamic where if you get a fail-to-launch situation, they understand. Because it happens—not every encounter leads to a touchdown.”

#5014. Australia lifts rates to 18-year high as AI boom, energy costs fuel inflation

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its benchmark rate to 4.85% on rising technology costs from AI investment and higher energy prices.

Australia’s central bank raised its interest rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, warning that inflation would stay elevated through much of 2027 as energy costs and AI-related investment added to price pressures.

The Reserve Bank of Australia’s monetary policy board voted 6–3 for the increase, with three members preferring to hold rates at 4.60%.

The bank pushed back its forecast for inflation to return to the top of its 2% to 3% target range until late 2027, around three quarters later than previously expected.

“AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods,” the board said, alongside higher fuel and commodity prices affected by the Middle East conflict. The interest rate in Australia is now at its highest level in 18 years.

“Today’s decision by the RBA was widely expected, but that doesn’t make it any easier for families and businesses,” said Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers. “It’s difficult news for many Australians who are already paying a hefty price for circumstances outside their control.”

The increase contrasts with the US Federal Reserve’s decision to hold rates last week, even as Fed officials have also warned that the AI investment boom is adding to price pressures, including for computer equipment and utilities.

#5012. Ethereum Privacy Network Aztec Rolls Out Major Security and Speed Upgrade

The Aztec Foundation said Tuesday that the upgrade, called Aztec Tierra and designated Alpha V6, delivers stronger security, formal verification of its proving system and faster deposits from Ethereum, alongside a refreshed brand.

Aztec is a decentralized layer-2 with more than 3,000 validators and fully programmable private smart contracts, and it pitches itself as having no privileged viewing keys or centralized sequencer, meaning no single operator can peer into or control user activity.

The upgrade resolves known vulnerabilities from earlier versions, including a critical issue discovered in V5, and adds extensive hardening. Notably, that includes a new AI-powered security testing harness and formal verification of core cryptographic components, a mathematical process for proving code behaves as intended.

The move reflects a broader scramble across crypto to harden code as AI tools make vulnerabilities easier to find.

On performance, Aztec said private transactions now generate client-side proofs in about one second on a standard device, twice as fast as before, while a new architecture cuts the time for Ethereum-to-Aztec messages from an average of two minutes to as little as 12 seconds, speeding up deposits and cross-chain activity.

The upgrade arrives with a crop of private applications spanning payments, trading, AI and social.

Leading them is zk.money, a private payments and savings app built by Aztec Labs that the team revived this year. With Tierra’s faster messaging, users can deposit directly from any Ethereum wallet without complex bridging.

Others in the lineup include Galactica for private AI inference, Nemi for private perpetuals trading, a private browser wallet called Nulo, and Rolling Chat, a private message board based on Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin’s own Aztec experiments.

#5010. Crypto.com to withdraw Hong Kong consumer app citing regulatory changes

Crypto.com will discontinue its consumer app services in Hong Kong in February next year.

Update (Nov. 3, 2026, 11:10 am UTC): This article has been updated to include comments from a Crypto.com spokesperson.

Crypto.com will discontinue its consumer app services in Hong Kong on Feb. 1, 2027, while continuing to pursue regulatory approval for its institutional exchange.

On Tuesday, a Crypto.com spokesperson told Cointelegraph that the company would discontinue its consumer app services in Hong Kong. The spokesperson said all affected customers had received advance notice and would receive instructions on closing their accounts and support to withdraw their funds.

According to local news outlet HK01, Crypto.com cited regulatory changes in emails sent to its users in Hong Kong. The consumer app is operated by Foris DAX MT Limited, while a separate entity, Foris DAX HK Limited, is seeking a Hong Kong virtual asset trading platform license.

According to the Securities and Futures Commission’s (SFC) public register, the company’s Hong Kong entity submitted its VATP license application on Feb. 9, 2024. Nearly three years later, Foris DAX HK Limited remains listed as “deemed-to-be-licensed” — a transitional status rather than full regulatory approval.

The spokesperson said the shutdown reflects Crypto.com’s efforts to optimize global operations and allocate resources toward sustainable long-term opportunities. However, the statement did not specify which regulatory changes prompted the decision.

Crypto.com also plans to continue pursuing the VATP license application for its institutional platform. The company said it remains committed to the broader Asia-Pacific region and working with regulators worldwide to support responsible industry growth.

Related: Hong Kong takes tokenized settlement to 24/7, plans stablecoin trials

#5008. This Serene 540-Square-Foot Apartment With Sweeping NYC Views Is Designed Down to an Eighth of an Inch

AD’s Small Spaces series is a celebration of small homes—1,000-square-feet or fewer!—with big design ideas. From Manhattan apartments to Milanese micro-homes, each one is proof that you don’t need a sprawling space to show off your personal style.

When a Los Angeles–based startup consultant decided to establish a more permanent foothold in New York, he searched for a place that felt different from his bright Southern California home. For him, being bicoastal meant embracing the best of each, and so, when in the Big Apple, he wanted the apartment to feel unmistakably like New York. That, he said, meant something “moodier, masculine, and more dramatic.” He landed on a Chelsea studio with sweeping views of the Empire State Building and Hudson Yards.

The 540-square-foot apartment, however, didn’t yet fit the bill. An oddly configured layout, coupled with a series of ad hoc renovations (including the discovery of a wall stuffed with Styrofoam), had left the space cramped and dated. That’s when Dyali, the studio founded by 2026 New American Voice Rahul Ghera, stepped in. Working within such a tight footprint, Ghera knew that every design element had to be exacting. The goal, he says, was “amplifying functionality day through evening”—from strategically placed storage to areas for entertaining friends and working comfortably from home.

In the living room of the Chelsea studio designed by Dyali, a rift oak coffee table from 1stDibs grounds the space, flanked by a 1960s armchair by Jindrich Halabala and a foldable chair by Carl Hansen & Son. A custom sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in linen runs along the wall, and a sand-colored rug by Nordic Knots unites the dining and living areas. The project construction is by Homlistic.

In the kitchen, walnut cabinetry is set off by a Calacatta Viola marble countertop from SMC Stone and a Dornbracht Elio fitting in stainless steel. Open shelving makes the room feel more spacious and everyday dishes are within reach.

“It’s almost like a hospitality project in a way—a personalized suite that’s your own place,” says Ghera. “Just with Jay-Z singing ‘I’m in New York’ views.”

A hotel-like emphasis on function guided the design. What began as a solution for storage unlocked one of the apartment’s defining features: a wall-to-wall cabinet running from the bedroom through the living room that doubles as a dresser and a place for games, books, and other odds and ends. To carry the cabinet through, Ghera widened an existing opening between the two rooms. Keeping the cabinet horizontal and continuous made the space feel “wider and bigger,” Ghera says, and drew the eye to the views and light from the windows. The horizon line where the cabinet meets the windowsill, he adds, is like a “border around the home” that almost “hugs you.”

The entry’s deep walnut closets and storage, Ghera says, “serve a pantry-like function,” holding items such as shoes, suitcases, linens, and cleaning supplies. “What I wanted to do is have that walnut turn the corner and just continue into the kitchen.” Courtney Heron’s painting of a domestic scene, Company at the Table, adds warmth to the space.

Ghera says he “intentionally wanted to create a dining feel,” while preserving the room’s openness. The lean form of the USM table allows you to “still see through it.” Audo’s Ready dining chairs in stained oak, upholstered in Audo bouclé, surround it. Beyond the table, a USM Haller cabinet in brown metal offers a casual perch for objets and sculpture, such as a Brutalist bronze sculpture from Mantiques Modern. Glassware, including a vintage Christian Dior ice bucket and lowball and highball glasses, rounds out the display.

The project, Ghera explains, was “an incredible puzzle to solve with a kind of quirky floor plan to start.” His answer was a restrained yet expressive material palette, anchored by rich walnut millwork and reflective surfaces that tie the rooms together. In the galley kitchen, a stainless-steel backsplash plays against the grain of the walnut cabinetry and lets the room feel more expansive than it is.

The millwork takes center stage in the bedroom, where a large custom mirror, bed, headboard, and nightstands, all in walnut, read as one cohesive piece. To make the most out of the existing square footage, Ghera opted for a platform bed and floating nightstands to avoid clutter and improve flow. A vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow in deep crimson, and bedding in shirt blue and red, add whimsy to the otherwise quiet room.

A walnut-framed mirror in the bedroom has an outsize effect. It “nearly doubled the square footage of what the apartment feels like,” says Ghera. “It continues the bouncing of light…and it just feels a little bit airier.”

The entry meets the client’s practical needs. A roomy storage cabinet in smoked oak from Ferm Living serves as a catchall for keys and everyday items, and a lacquered wood mirror from West Elm leans against the wall beside a burgundy linen ottoman from de Le Cuona.

Floating night tables and a custom cabinet along the window provide ample storage. Bedside, Stemlite table lamps in pebble gray by Gubi softly illuminate the space. Sara Marlowe Hall’s pastel drawings, Red 1 & Red 2, play off the crimson vintage Turkish kilim lumbar pillow

In the living room, comfort and flexibility were musts. The client, who likes to host friends for drinks or dinner, needed a space that could easily adapt to gatherings of varying sizes. A custom, deep-seated sofa upholstered in Larsen’s Asante in Linen fabric fits several guests and offers a cozy spot for overnight visitors. Versatile furnishings like the Cuba Lounge Chair by Carl Hansen & Son can be folded up and tucked away in the closet to make room for larger parties.

Fitting a dining area into a studio of this size was a true exercise in spatial gymnastics. “It still kind of blows my mind,” says Ghera, “but it works.” A sleek USM dining table topped with oak veneer forms its own “contained” island where a suspension lamp hangs deliberately low to serve as a “focal point,” Ghera says.

Rather than fret over the windowless bathroom, Ghera chose to “lean into it.” “Small rooms look incredible when they’re a little darker,” he says. Outer Clé’s Lido Aperto Bouchon tiles in matte rare garnet wrap the space, and a custom sink pairs Calacatta Viola marble with a stainless-steel base, made from “every square inch” of the stone used in the kitchen.

As a friend told the client, the “pièce de résistance” of the apartment is the bathroom, and he couldn’t agree more. Oxblood garnet tiles envelop the space, from floor to ceiling. Lighting spills from above and below the medicine cabinet and washes down from a cove in the shower. “It really just feels like you are cradled in this space,” says Ghera. “It’s a little sexy.” Reeded glass adds a hint of transparency. “It’s like showering in the world’s coolest hotel,” says the client.

Working within the constraints of such a small studio left little margin for error. Rather than letting it faze him, Ghera worked “down to the eighth of an inch,” he says. “You really have to be so honed in on the tiny details…and intentional about the things you do.”

#5006. BlackRock’s IBIT sees biggest Bitcoin ETF outflows since June

BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF shed $405.3 million on Monday as US spot Bitcoin funds opened November with nearly $399 million in net outflows.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) recorded its largest daily outflow since June on Monday as US-listed spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) kicked off November with further withdrawals.

The funds recorded $398.6 million in net outflows, led by $405.3 million from IBIT, according to Farside Investors data.

IBIT’s outflow was its largest since June 26, when investors pulled $444.5 million. Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC) attracted $6.7 million on Monday, partially offsetting the outflows.

The withdrawals followed $515 million in net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs in October. The funds have recorded around $38 million in net outflows so far in 2026.

“I wouldn’t interpret these outflows as a rejection of digital assets,” Edwin Mata, CEO of tokenization company Brickken, said in commentary published Monday. “Investors reduce exposure when uncertainty rises, particularly after an event that raises questions about the security of market infrastructure.”

The withdrawals came amid broader crypto market volatility following the $6.3 billion Binance hack.

Bitcoin briefly fell below $76,400 on Monday, its lowest level since August, according to CoinGecko. The cryptocurrency traded at around $76,600 at publication, down 3.7% over the past seven days.

US spot Ether (ETH) ETFs also recorded about $140 million in net outflows on Monday, extending their losing streak to six trading days after posting a record $1.61 billion in monthly outflows in October, according to SoSoValue data.

Designer Lisa Shaffer, AD PRO Senior Editor Mel Studach, designer Alexa Hampton, Theodore Alexander President Ed Taplitz, designer Rasheeda Gray, and Theodore Alexander VP of Marketing Sydney Wells Martin.

Over cocktails, wood-fired pizzas, and live music, guests hobnobbed, swapped notes on Market, and celebrated the brand’s remarkable legacy. As they departed, they were gifted that signature Pentreath chair—a miniature keychain version, cast in polished brass—a charming symbol of the decades to come.

#5003. Kraken restricts accounts amid suspected $133M EU crypto theft

Crypto.com also took steps to block funds tied to the suspected theft, while Kraken said its systems and customer accounts were not compromised.

Update (Nov. 3, 2026, 11:51 am UTC): This article has been updated with a revised headline and responses from Kraken, OKX and Crypto.com.

Kraken has restricted accounts linked to a suspected crypto theft of more than $133 million from an unidentified European Union entity and is working with law enforcement to support recovery efforts.

“This incident did not originate on the Kraken platform, and we’re actively investigating reports that some of the assets were subsequently moved through accounts on our platform,” Kraken told Cointelegraph. “We’ve restricted the accounts in question and are working with law enforcement to support recovery efforts.”

Kraken’s statement follows blockchain investigator ZachXBT’s disclosure on Tuesday that he identified another $27 million in withdrawals from centralized exchanges, increasing the suspected losses from the $106 million he reported on Monday. He said some withdrawals occurred after his initial disclosure.

Bitquery reported that the suspected stolen funds were withdrawn from accounts at Kraken, Crypto.com and OKX. It also found that $62.98 million in stablecoins was converted into 27,553 Ether (ETH) within roughly four hours.

Kraken said its security systems had not been compromised, no customer accounts had been taken over and there was no ongoing risk to its customers.

Crypto.com told Cointelegraph that it had taken steps to prevent funds associated with the incident from moving through its platform.

“We are aware of this report and have taken appropriate action to block any funds associated with this third-party incident from moving through Crypto.com,” a spokesperson said. “Our platform remains fully operational, and all user funds are secure and accessible.”

OKX acknowledged Cointelegraph’s request for comment and said it was looking into the matter.

As of 13:47 UTC Monday, approximately $78.3 million remained in wallets linked to the suspected attacker, while $30.5 million had moved out of the tracked addresses, according to Bitquery. Only $3.74 million remained in USDC that issuer Circle could potentially freeze, while Tether had already frozen $1.1 million in USDT.

“My working theory is a large financial institution in Western Europe was exploited and it’s currently being covered up,” ZachXBT said on his Telegram channel.

He also said the lack of a proper incident disclosure allowed more than $30 million to be laundered, claiming EU law enforcement could otherwise have frozen the funds. The victim’s identity and allegations of a cover-up remain unverified.

ZachXBT said earlier that the attacker was swapping funds into ETH and Monero (XMR) through instant exchanges and cross-chain bridges. He said the laundering patterns did not match those typically used by North Korea’s Lazarus Group.
