#4948. 9 Decorative Plates for When You’re Sick of Boring Dishes (2026)

The great thing about decorative plates is that they don’t have to disappear into storage once dinner is over. Hang a few on a display wall, prop one up alongside your favorite cookbooks, or work it into a shelf vignette. So what makes one worth showing off? It’s the details that spark curiosity: A scalloped edge, an unexpected color combination, or a hand-painted pattern can be enough to make you look twice. “Any plate with a fun decorative motif, bright colors, or an interesting shape makes it more than just simply functional,” says Olympia Irving of Carolina Irving and Daughters.

Of course, good looks are only part of the appeal. The most memorable pieces often have a story to tell, whether it's a vintage find or a handmade design with charming, artisanal characteristics. Even the finish can make a statement. “I often find myself drawn to surfaces that look like they’re in flux—glazes that pool unpredictably or finishes that suggest movement or fragility, even in solid materials," says Anna Jewsbury, founder and artistic director of Completedworks.

There's no need to play by the rules of a perfectly coordinated table setting. A little contrast, a playful border, or a beautifully imperfect finish makes for a more interesting table—one that looks like it can only belong to you. Ahead, nine decorative plates that deserve a spot in your regular rotation and perhaps a prime position in your china cabinet.

For a plate that has lived a completely different life before landing on your table—try this Completedworks dinner plate made from recycled glass. Sculptural and subversive, it’s made from broken windows, melted glass bottles, and is repurposed using old engine oil as fuel. “We often play with the illusion of softness in materials that are anything but. Those moments where form and material are at odds are the ones I find most compelling,” Jewsbury shares.

Transport yourself to the French countryside with this Villeroy & Boch dinner plate. Part of the brand's beloved French Garden collection, its fruit-and-floral motif brings to mind sun-drenched afternoons and leisurely lunches in the garden. Even fruit and pastries straight from the market become a proper breakfast spread.

Does anything scream summer more than seashell-shaped splatterware? These Concha plates by editor-favorite brand Carolina Irving & Daughters bring together a seaside-inspired shape along with a creative, painterly glaze. “It is easy to make a table setting pop by only adding a few decorative touches, whether that is a dessert plate or a salt dish,” Irving says. “Truthfully, we love to use decorative plates as our everyday dishware!”

Designed by Cabana and made by heritage Italian porcelain house Ginori 1735, the painterly motif on this plate adds an element of rustic Italian charm to the table. Whether you stick to a cohesive set or play around with different colors and patterns for a more collected vibe, these plates can make even the simplest meals feel storied.

Score a vintage-inspired find without the hours spent scouring antique shops. Olive Ateliers did the legwork with its Vincent Plate, featuring a hand-painted floral motif, an aged blue rim, and an ivory ceramic base. “A plate becomes more when it holds history,” shares Laura Sotelo, cofounder of Olive Ateliers. “The wow isn’t about perfection—it’s about the story it carries. It should feel like it belonged somewhere long before it ended up in your hands.”

Each plate is finished by hand, giving it the character of a one-of-a-kind discovery. One important distinction: This plate isn't food-safe, so save it for a spot on your wall or shelf instead.

The soft pale yellow tones and the scalloped edge are some of our favorite details about these affordable, vintage-inspired dinner plates by West Elm. They are perfect for those who want to dip their toes into a decorative tabletop but aren’t quite ready to splurge. Sold in sets of four or eight, they strike the right balance between charm and accessibility and are ideal for daily use.

Your next dinner party can channel a little Italian holiday spirit with these hand-painted plates, crafted in a family-run workshop on the Amalfi Coast. They're available in two sizes, so they're equally charming piled high with antipasti or passed around the table with the main course.

A collaboration between L’Objet and South African artist Ruan Hoffmann, this plate brings a bold edge to the table with its painterly design and hand-applied 24k gold accents. While it’s smaller in dimension (6.5 inches), it makes a subtle statement and can complement your existing dinnerware.

If you're a fan of British artist Tess Newall's painterly work, you'll be happy to know her designs have made their way to the dinner table, courtesy of Porta. The “Ottoline” plates take inspiration from English country houses, Bloomsbury interiors, and traditional European ceramics. These hand-painted pieces are adorned with scrolling motifs, dotted edges, and wave detailing in contrasting shades of slate blue and rust. Sold in sets of four, they're a lovely way to bring a little art history to the table.

#4943. Where Does Mark Ruffalo Live? Exploring the Avengers Star’s East Coast Real Estate Portfolio

He’s currently booked and busy, but where does Mark Ruffalo live when he’s not filming? The Oscar-nominated actor appears in five projects released in 2026 alone. With that kind of schedule, the Marvel star must maintain somewhat of a nomadic lifestyle. It’s no surprise that, for years, he and his family juggled properties on both coasts. These days, however, Ruffalo is all in on New York—when he isn’t traveling to movie sets around the world.

Read on to learn more about the Emmy winner’s homes in the Big Apple and beyond.

Ruffalo first visited the small town of Callicoon in New York’s Catskills region in the mid-’90s, according to a December 2017 interview with Men’s Journal. Soon after visiting Callicoon, the 28-year-old Ruffalo paid $63,000 for his first home there: a 27-acre property with a one-room cabin. Around 2001, he and his wife, Sunrise Coigney, purchased an estate there, on a former dairy farm, complete with a 19th-century post-and-beam barn. “Smartest thing I ever did,” the Avengers star told the outlet. “It ended up having a huge influence on my life in many ways.”

At first, Ruffalo and his family split their time between their Los Angeles and New York homes. But that soon began to wear on the couple, spurring the decision to sell their Hollywood Hills property in 2009 and move to Callicoon full-time. “The whole guiding idea for living upstate was to simplify,” Ruffalo said in 2011. “It’s the best thing I could have done for the family as a whole and for the kids in particular.… We’re letting them grow a little wild, and we step in when it’s essential, but in a lot of ways they figure stuff out on their own and they do it in a way that’s organic and lasts. We live in a small space and we’re really influenced by the natural world around us. Eventually that is reflected in one’s behavior and how you get along with other people. There’s a lot of quiet in the country and there’s a lot of quietness in my children.”

On the farm, the Now You See Me actor built a woodworking shop, a chicken coop, and a garden where he grows “strawberries, rhubarb, tomatoes, basil, corn, a beautiful asparagus bed that’s five years old, and watermelon, which is hard to grow up here,” Ruffalo said. “Now I’m doing a little orchard—raspberries, Honeycrisp apples, blueberries, a pear tree.”

In the mid-2010s, Ruffalo moved his primary residence back to NYC for his children’s schooling. “We try to get to our place in Callicoon as much as we can on weekends and holidays and of course spend the summer there,” he said in 2016. “It’s a place I will always hold dear to my heart, filled with lifetime friends and lots of positive sentiment. It’s the best, most-interlocked community I have ever lived in save for my early years in Los Angeles when I was scraping it out to become an actor.” Ruffalo also compared the region to his upbringing in Wisconsin: “Just outside my town there were vast dairy farms, where I would spend my days as a boy fishing in creeks and ponds or climbing around in trees. Everything about the Catskills reminds me of my childhood. I don’t know what to say other than it’s my home.”

Ruffalo and Coigney were married in 2000 and welcomed the first of three children the following year. In December 2004, a few months before their second child was born, the growing family moved into a three-bedroom Hollywood Hills home that they bought for about $1.7 million. It was the cherry on top of a banner year for Ruffalo, who appeared in four movies that year: We Don’t Live Here Anymore, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, 13 Going on 30, and Collateral.

According to The Los Angeles Times, the gated single-story residence dated to 1933 and was built in the style of a Connecticut farmhouse. Across 3,000 square feet, it hosted three bedrooms, four bathrooms, and a detached guesthouse. Highlights included a fireplace-warmed living room with beamed ceilings, and a breakfast room.

Ruffalo and Coigney welcomed their third child in 2007, then sold the Los Angeles house for $1.65 million two years later to New Girl star Zooey Deschanel and her then husband, Death Cab for Cutie frontman Ben Gibbard. Deschanel and Gibbard divorced in 2012, and Deschanel sold the property in 2015, the Los Angeles Times reported.

Ruffalo’s next real estate purchase was a $3.5 million town house in Brooklyn’s Carroll Gardens neighborhood in 2015. Spanning 3,000 square feet, the 1899-built residence had four bedrooms, three bathrooms, a backyard garden, and dreamy period details: cathedral ceilings, marble fireplaces, decorative arches, and wide-plank wood flooring. There was also a large kitchen with a high-end range, a sunroom with a balcony, and a curved wooden staircase leading to the upstairs bedrooms.

The actor sold the Brooklyn home in 2017 for $3.2 million—a slight loss.

Mark Ruffalo at a rally for the Landmark West Park Presbyterian Church in 2025

Though he left Brooklyn, Ruffalo was not leaving NYC altogether—just moving across the river to Manhattan. In January 2017, he and Coigney were seen touring a $9.99 million six-bedroom town house on the Upper West Side. While it doesn’t appear that they signed that deed, the couple did pick up a home in the neighborhood at some point thereafter. The Poor Things star has been a vocal supporter of upholding the landmark status of the neighborhood’s historic West Park Presbyterian Church since 2023. In December 2025, he said that he lived “a block away from the church.” While the details of this real estate transaction are unknown, Ruffalo’s Upper West Side residence is reportedly an early-20th-century four-story town house.

#4939. 7 Best Lumbar Pillows Bolster Your Back and Bedscape (2026)

Though a lumbar pillow is typically the last detail in making a bed, it’s often the first thing you or a guest will notice. Because it’s long and low, its best suited to the space in front of loftier throw pillows, making a horizon line across your bedscape, and it can bring in a color or texture the rest of the room is vying for. The shape turns up all over AD’s archives, including in supermodel Paloma Elsesser’s Brooklyn home and this classically decorated Southern house.

A lumbar pillow can mean two things: a firm or cushioned gel pillow designed to support the lower back, or an elegant decorative detail among your bedding. While we like both, we’ll leave the Cushion Lab’s best-of for another day. Here, we’re focused on a more inspirational lineup, between linen, wool, velvet, and cotton lumbar pillows that pull a bed and sofa together (and still give your lower back something to lean on in an accent chair). Below are the seven we like best.

Sometimes one pillow is all a bed really needs. West Elm’s oversized linen pillow cover has the scale to anchor a queen or king bed on its own, creating a clean, pulled-together look without a full stack of throw pillows. The linen keeps it loose, making it especially well-suited to coastal, minimalist, modern farmhouse, and casual contemporary spaces.

This pillow is all about texture. Its dimensional surface gives a sofa or bed a more layered, considered look without relying on a loud print or saturated color. In other words, its style will speak volumes even when paired with quieter neutrals.

At 48 inches, Quince’s velvet lumbar is long enough to span a queen bed with nothing else in front of it, and the cotton pile catches light in a way linen won’t. The glacier blue reads cool and a little silvery against white or oatmeal bedding. It’s dry clean only, and the insert is sold separately.

Color is the point with this Athena cushion. Rather than fading quietly into the background, this lumbar pillow is designed to bring energy to a room, whether it’s breaking up the monotony of a neutral living room or adding contrast to a more restrained bedding scheme. It’s the kind of accent that makes a pillow arrangement feel more collected, playful, and intentional.

A little color can go a long way, especially in the form of Pendleton’s Turquoise Crosses Lumbar Pillow. Its vivid palette and geometric pattern give neutral furniture or a plain accent chair an instant lift. For anyone drawn to Southwestern-inspired textiles, this pick brings just enough graphic punch without crowding the rest of the room.

The Mendocino cover is made up of hand-dyed washed linen, so the color shifts slightly across the surface instead of sitting flat. What separates it from the other linen picks here is the fringe: three-inch knotted tassels run along two sides, which give a simple lumbar some movement at the ends of a sofa or bed. Nota bene: the insert is sold separately.

Washed linen has a way of making a room feel more relaxed and breezy, which is exactly the appeal of Brooklinen’s pillow cover. The simple design is easy to fold into an existing pillow arrangement, while the softly textured fabric and choice of vibrant hues keep it from feeling too plain.

A lumbar pillow is a long, rectangular cushion designed to support the lower back. The term describes two different products: one is the ergonomic back support pillow, often memory foam, made for an office chair or car seat. The other is the decorative version on this list, which works as an accent piece on beds, sofas, benches, and accent chairs. Their shape makes them especially useful for layering with standard square throw pillows, adding dimension without making a space feel cluttered.

One of the easiest ways to style a lumbar pillow is to place it in front of larger pillows or shams on a bed. On a sofa or accent chair, a lumbar pillow can serve as a single focal point or be paired with smaller throw pillows in complementary colors, patterns, or textures. For a more polished look, choose a lumbar pillow that either picks up a color already in the room or brings in a contrasting texture, like linen, wool, velvet, or tassels.

For lower back support, a lumbar pillow goes in the curve between your back and the back of a sofa, reading chair, or recliner chair. Keep in mind a firmer, fuller back pillow will likely do more for your posture than a soft, decorative one. For styling, it can also be centered across a bed, layered in front of sleeping pillows, or placed on a bench for extra comfort and visual interest. Oversized lumbar pillows work especially well on queen and king beds because they can anchor the entire pillow arrangement with one clean horizontal line.

#4938. The Cultural Unconscious May Explain Why Things Feel Bleak

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

Recently, many patients have expressed that things feel heavy and bleak now in the world. There seems to be “something in the air.” What they’re speaking to is a general cultural angst whereby people feel grim about a lot of things—the economy, racism, sexual violence, politics, the environment, and more. This cultural angst is the felt mood or experience of our times. While not everyone feels somber, my patients are naming something real.

The American Psychological Association’s 2026 Stress in America report found that 74 percent of adults identified the future of the nation as a significant source of stress. The shared sense of unease, dread, or anxiety about the direction of our society has numerous sources that may be understood as a crisis of trust.

Societal advancements like artificial intelligence (AI) and social media fuel excitement, coupled with skepticism or disdain because it’s no longer entirely clear what’s real or true. These same advancements are liberating in their efficiency, yet they push us to simplify through reaction buttons and character limits. Nuance flattens, reflection and discernment can be compromised, and there may be no time or space for complexity. That becomes the background layer of our cultural experience, forming what we call “the cultural unconscious.”

You have likely heard about the personal unconscious—an individual’s memories, experiences, and perceptions that are forgotten, repressed, dissociated, or never fully registered but still leave an imprint. Perhaps you’ve heard of the collective unconscious, a shared psychological inheritance. It’s a reservoir of collective patterns, instincts, and experiences around what it means to be human, regardless of the time or place.

Lesser known is the concept of the “cultural unconscious,” the psychic space between the personal and the collective. It’s less universal than the collective unconscious but broader than the personal unconscious. Essentially, it bridges the two. Often, when we speak of culture, we mean what we're aware of—think celebrities, lingo, and touchstones like 9/11. However, culture also has an unconscious aspect, often reflected in intense emotional responses.

The cultural unconscious is a collection of shared images, concerns, and unprocessed material in a group's psyche. It can activate at the same time across many people, explaining why certain news stories, topics, and trends spread like wildfire, and everyone wants to weigh in.

In both the Lindsay Clancy case and the Cornell 7 case, many respond with their personal stories. These news pieces have activated the cultural unconscious partially because they touch shared archetypes and experiences—that of the good/bad mother and also the all-too-common experience of sexual violence. Approximately 800 people are harmed by sexual violence daily, according to RAINN, the anti-sexual violence organization and operator of the National Sexual Assault Hotline.1 And sexual violence is not limited to a particular gender, meaning almost everyone either experiences it themselves or knows someone who has.

When a charged issue, such as sexual violence, touches the culture, many people become activated, or, in common parlance, feel “triggered” or “dysregulated.” My colleagues, psychiatrist and Jungian analyst Thomas Singer, and psychologist and Jungian analyst Sam Kimbles, identified and developed scholarship on “cultural complexes.”2 Just as a person can feel “taken over” by a complex (which you can read about in relation to the mother complex, feeling triggered, and the father complex), so, too, can a culture be taken over.

A reminder: Complexes are triggered by certain themes, carry strong emotion, act with autonomy, and pull people into reactions they can't easily step back from. With a cultural complex, it takes hold of the people who comprise a group. When many are activated, it shows up in collective behavior, such as public outrage, scapegoating, polarization, or dogmatism.

We are struggling culturally to tolerate ambiguity and complexity, especially psychological complexity. Instead of holding conflicting realities, we hunker down with diagnoses, moral judgments, polarized views, and “all-good, all-bad” places. I am not asserting that diagnoses lack validity or that objective distinctions between good and bad behavior don't exist. Rather, I emphasize how certainty in judgment, labels, and categories can be defensive, protecting us from discomfort and quelling our anxieties, especially during these charged times, while foreclosing reflection, curiosity, and understanding.

We live in cultural times where commentary and judgment dominate over reflection and understanding; where certainty is valued over curiosity. When we feel overwhelmed, overstimulated, and unsure about our cultural reality, we don’t contain it. It develops into a crisis of psychological containment and gets enacted through splitting, projection, intolerance, rigidity, and polarization. It manifests as a specific cultural complex such as the victim-perpetrator complex. To be clear, there are victims and perpetrators. Real harms have occurred, and we cannot brush them aside under the guise of a psychological mechanism. But the way it seizes the culture with such intensity suggests a complex is activating culturally.

People who have no connection to Lindsay Clancy or the Cornell 7 are expressing exceptionally strong opinions. Why? One explanation is that culturally, we haven’t learned to hold or integrate both poles of the victim-perpetrator complex. It can be easier to identify with one pole and disown the other—for instance, avoiding our own capacity for harm or “perpetration” or, conversely, our own vulnerability or “victimization.”

When these news stories arise, many people project their disowned self onto the “other,” which is why some call the Cornell 7 “monsters,” while Jane Doe is being ripped to shreds and receiving death threats. Each side is treated wholly as “right” or “justified,” rather than recognizing that humans are complicated and nuanced. Anyone who complicates the picture or raises those points feels threatening to people in the throes of the victim-perpetrator complex.

I am not challenging the desire for justice or accountability. I am drawing attention to the psychological toll of the cultural angst expressed through the complex, evident in the rigidity, intensity, speed, and attitude of total certainty. Such reactions diminish our capacity to embrace ambiguity and complexity, and to recognize there may be more than two sides to a story.

One path forward is to begin recognizing and relating to the grip of cultural complexes—in this case, holding both poles of the victim-perpetrator complex. Each of us contains some capacity for vulnerability and for harm. Relating to each side of the cultural complex is a first step. Overidentifying with one pole of the complex does no one any good and often makes the world feel heavier and grim. To counter that, we need nuance and discernment. Yes, the world can be heavy, but it can also be light and joyful. You can acknowledge one while not discounting the other.

1. Sexual Violence Statistics - RAINN. (2025, June 12). Rainn. https://rainn.org/get-informed/sexual-violence-statistics/

2. Singer, T. (2006). The cultural complex: a statement of the theory and its application. Psychotherapy & Politics International, 4(3). Retrieved from https://ojs.aut.ac.nz/psychotherapy-politics-international/article/view…

#4933. Skeleton Architecture: 7 Buildings That Prove Why Bones Are Some Designer’s Favorite Muse

“It should be harsh and cruel, as if made of bones,” Antoni Gaudí wrote next to his sketch of the Passion Façade, the west-facing entrance of his magnum opus, the Sagrada Família. In stark contrast to the organic, pictorial design of the Nativity Façade on the opposite side of the basilica, which depicts the birth of Jesus, Gaudí employed skeletal forms to evoke human suffering and Christ’s final days.

While the Catalan architect drew inspiration from skeletons for multiple projects—most notably Barcelona’s Casa Batlló, a residential building known as the House of Bones for its dragon-vertebrae-inspired design, and Casa Milà, with its undulating, rib cage–like arches—he was not the first to do so. Skeletons have long served as sacred ornamentation across cultures, representing the transience of life. As early as 7,200 BCE, Middle Eastern communities displayed human skulls in domestic spaces to honor their ancestors, while in Mesoamerica, the Aztecs erected elaborate skull racks known as tzompantli to display sacrificial captives’ remains as a demonstration of power. Following the Black Death in medieval Europe, memento mori, symbolic reminders of death’s inevitability, further ubiquitized skulls in art and architecture. Meanwhile, as European cemeteries became increasingly inundated from the Middle Ages into the early modern period, carcasses were exhumed and relocated to crypts featuring skeletal decorative displays, such as Portugal’s 16th-century Capela dos Ossos and the Czech Republic’s Sedlec Ossuary.

By the late 19th and early 20th centuries, architects such as Antoni Gaudí began studying skeletal anatomy not merely for adornment, but as the actual framework for buildings. After all, much like the human body, a building relies on its skeleton as the foundation for life within. From an avant-garde temple to to contemporary buildings constructed to resemble skeletal forms, below are architectural marvels that reveal why skeletons remain an enduring muse for architects.

While historic ossuaries incorporated actual human remains into their architecture, contemporary designer and artist Chalermchai Kositpipat incorporated ornamental skeletal architecture into Wat Rong Khun, or the White Temple, an unconventional Buddhist temple and art installation that depicts the stages of Nirvana. To enter the temple, visitors must cross a bridge over a sea of sculpted hands and skulls, symbolizing human desire and the cycle of suffering on the path to enlightenment. Started in 1997 and still evolving, the complex features intricate white ornamentation and mirrored glass symbolizing purity and wisdom.

Moving beyond skeletal ornamentation, Antoni Gaudí helped pioneer Catalan Modernism, a late 19th- and early 20th-century architectural movement that challenged traditional academicism, rejecting rigid geometry in favor of nature’s organic forms and structural principles, including those of skeletal anatomy. Nicknamed the House of Bones, Gaudí’s Casa Batlló, which was created from 1904–1906, is among the most prominent examples of this movement. Its undulating façade features balconies resembling skulls, slender bone-like columns, and a roof covered in iridescent scales that evokes a dragon’s spine. Originally designed as a private residence for textile industrialist Josep Batlló, the UNESCO-listed building is now a museum open to visitors, its skeletal framework inspiring interpretations ranging from human anatomy to the legend of Saint George slaying the dragon.

Built between 1906 and 1912, another of Gaudí’s architectural masterpieces, Casa Milà, also known as La Pedrera, draws inspiration from natural forms, most notably in what’s known as the Whale-Bone Attic, where 270 repeating brick arches expand and contract in size to resemble the rib cage of a giant whale. These catenary arches support the building’s rippling roof, demonstrating Gaudí’s fascination with the relationship between anatomy and engineering. More broadly, Gaudí conceived the building as an animal body, with internal supporting columns serving as its bones and the sculptural stone façade as its skin. Originally constructed as a residential apartment building, the UNESCO World Heritage Site remains partly residential, while its attic, rooftop with surreal sculptural chimneys, and other historic spaces are open to visitors.

Designed by Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava and completed in 1994, the Lyon-Saint Exupéry Airport Railway Station combines skeletal engineering with the imagery of a bird taking flight. “Sometimes I say [I’m inspired by] the human skeleton, because it’s true that there’s something essential in the construction of our body,” Calatrava once told Fast Company in 2010. (He’s also inspired by nature more broadly, he added.)

This idea is on full display at the Lyon-Saint Exupéry Airport Railway Station, where the expansive central hall features a soaring steel framework of intersecting arches, while the adjoining railway platforms are sheltered beneath a vaulted concrete roof supported by rib-like structures. The building’s curved, tapering spine and wing-shaped silhouette evoke avian anatomy.

Another Calatrava design, the Quadracci Pavilion at the Milwaukee Art Museum, completed in 2001, emulates a mythical winged skeletal form. Its soaring Windhover Hall features repeating white concrete ribs, pointed arches, and a 90-foot-high glass ceiling, evoking a Gothic cathedral with the anatomy of a fantastical creature. Outside, the building’s most recognizable feature, the Burke Brise Soleil, consists of 72 steel fins that open and close like enormous wings, spanning 217 feet when fully extended.

The World Trade Center Oculus resembles an enormous skeletal structure through its repeating white steel ribs, which extend outward to form a pair of wing-like canopies. Another Calatrava project, the architect conceived it as a symbol of hope and renewal following the September 11 attacks—the transportation hub was inspired by the image of a bird being released from a child’s hands. Inside, its soaring, cathedral-like hall features an elliptical framework of steel and glass, with a central skylight that floods the space with natural light. The structure’s combination of skeletal anatomy and avian symbolism is one of the most renowned projects embodying Calatrava’s exploration of biological forms in architecture.

The 61,000 meter headquarters for Chinese fashion company Xinhee, designed by Beijing-based MAD Architects and opened in 2017, conjures the architecture of the human body. Conceived of as a structure of “skin and bones,” the building features a diagonal steel skeleton enveloped in translucent PTFE membrane resembling fabric draped over the human body, while also filtering natural light and facilitating natural ventilation in the subtropical climate. Its flower-like layout consists of six radiating wings, each housing a different atrium, which are connected by a suspended footbridge that doubles as a fashion runway. With its elevated gardens and multistory green spaces, the structure integrates nature into the building’s skeletal framework. Known as one of the most innovative buildings in contemporary China, the design personifies the relationship between fashion and architecture.

#4929. Parental Alienation: Recognizing the Signs Early

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

You never thought it could happen to you. Divorce is difficult, but losing the bond with your children is excruciating. You may be the emotionally available parent who has done the bulk of the "real" parenting since your children were born, and your bond has always been strong. Yet, your kids are suddenly cold and rude to you. They avoid being around you and refuse to tell you anything about their life. When you ask if your co-parent is behind their treatment, they become irate and refuse to even speak to you. It is soul-crushing.

Although there can be many reasons for a child's withdrawal from a parent during a divorce, there is a certain type of co-parent who intentionally undermines the opposite parent's relationship with the children. Often, it starts with a co-parent who is emotionally immature and cannot lose face. They strive, always, to protect their ego. Their image means everything to them, so after a divorce, they must come out on top. In addition, this parent, who may lack emotional availability, is often exceedingly jealous of the parent who is emotionally available and who has an authentically close bond with the kids—so they seek to sabotage it. Parental alienation is insidious. So, understanding how it works is critical when attempting to salvage your relationship with your kids.

Picture yourself on the back of a boat in the ocean with your child and co-parent. Your child holds the only life preserver. You and your co-parent are thrown out of the boat in different directions. Thrashing in the water, your co-parent begins to wail to the child, “I am not going to make it! I’m not going to make it! Help me!” Although you are also struggling, you tell your child, “Stay in the boat, honey! Don’t let go of that life preserver. Stay where you are.” But your child is completely panicked by your co-parent's screams, so they jump in the water to try to help them.

As your child and co-parent climb back into the boat, your co-parent says to your child, “I would not have made it without you. I would not be here without you. What would I ever do without you?”

In this scenario, a couple of things are happening. First, your co-parent is playing the victim, and by doing so, sends your child into an intense panic. Kids are psychologically, neurologically, genetically, physiologically, and emotionally programmed to protect their attachment relationship, so when an attachment figure says they do not know if they are going to make it, the child instinctively dives in to help them. The child may ignore their own health, well-being, and emotional needs to take care of their parent, so they do not lose this parent. Second, when the co-parent and child get back to safer ground, the co-parent says something that makes the child believe that they are the only one who can help this co-parent in difficult times, just like they did. That they are this parent’s “lifeline,” so to speak.

Alternatively, you strive to be your child’s protector, not the other way around. You can take care of your own emotional needs and would never burden your child with them. This may be additional evidence that you are an emotionally healthy parent.

When your child is alienated, they lose their innocence and ability to be a kid because they are consumed with worry about the parent who acts as if they will not survive the “mistreatment” that you are inflicting. This child is burdened by the responsibility of holding your co-parent up. And guess what? Your co-parent exploits this. When the child is disloyal to you, the co-parent acts as if their mental health is repaired, and everything is right in the world. The child feels unburdened from worry for a moment. Naturally, the child then looks for more opportunities to display and discuss their rejection of you so they can continue to relieve themselves of the anxiety that comes from feeling responsible for a parent’s well-being. Your co-parent rewards the child and continues to inappropriately confide in the child about how “unfair” and “devious” you are, improperly sharing adult information.

You are locked out of their life, and it may be the worst pain that you have ever felt. Yet, the more you try to get your child to see the manipulation, the more your child sees you as the “bully” that the co-parent has mischaracterized you as. You feel helpless and hopeless.

You collect data about your co-parent’s emotional mistreatment and negligence, yet every time you bring something up in court, your co-parent denies it and accuses you of worse. The battles in court last for months and years with no real progress. So, what can you do?

One option is to let your attorney work from the outside in, while you work from the inside out. Focus on rehabilitating your bond, not stopping your co-parent. As an emotionally available parent, you may have important parenting skills that your co-parent seems to lack. You can empathize instead of sympathizing. You can understand a different perspective and honor it. Flexibility comes easy to you, and so does constructively working out conflict. And, most importantly, you can follow through with a boundary or limit in a calm and loving manner.

Additionally, if you are the emotionally invested parent, you may remember the endearing, hilarious, and adorable moments when your child did something incredibly special at a very young age. Your co-parent may not. Patiently waiting for a natural moment to retell a story about your child saving a baby bird when he was 3 or standing up to the neighborhood bully to protect her younger sibling are ways to prove to your child that you have always been there for them and that you have always seen them.

Seize every moment to do the emotionally intelligent things that your co-parent usually cannot do, and never point them out. Allow the child to feel the emotional safety that you provide when they are with you. They may be able to begin to discern how different they feel when they are with your co-parent. Most importantly, never ever give up. You can find more information on this topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist: Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control, at Home, at Work, and In Life.

#4927. Where to Buy Vintage Lamps (2026): 1stDibs, Etsy, and More

Listen—we’ve all fallen prey to the sort of lighting lethargy that keeps our hastily-purchased mass market table lamps on our bedside. A fluorescent task lamp might still hover over the couch, a garish flush mount shedding its harsh light. So why a vintage lamp? Because it indicates you thought about your lighting instead of going the route of a last-minute, add-to-cart impulse buy. This was deliberately searched and purchased. This was a choice made with historical design context in mind, whether it’s midcentury modern, Art Deco, or Hollywood Regency. A carefully considered piece of lighting shows your home decor chops—you’ve gone above and beyond the look of the room to consider the vibe of the room. A magnificent vintage piece communicates all that. We rounded up a few retailer options to find just the thing you need for a living room revamp, a ceiling light overhaul, or a lampshade upgrade.

We pull from 1stDibs regularly when shopping out our various home tours, where we can find the iconic works sprinkled throughout the homes of celebrities, designers, and celebrity designers. A Charlotte Perriand sconce indicates at least one substantial coffee book on the oeuvre of Le Corbusier is nearby, and a reissue of the 1960’s Gelato lamp by Italian designer Carlo Nason’s are just the tip of the iceberg. In other words: Design dorks will delight in this catalog of artifacts and iconic pieces.

Etsy is a go-to when you’re searching for a vibe rather than a specific model or designer. Try keyword searching for terms like “Art Deco” or “ginger jar lamp” and a trove of collectibles, like thrift-store-friendly finds and veritable antique gems, will surface in search. The online marketplace’s vast web of sellers means a library of vintage lighting that spans centuries and styles, often times for less than what you’d find at places like 1st Dibs and Chairish since sellers choose what they price for shipping. Contributor Lori Keong has had good luck buying pieces there from across the pond in the UK and even further afield in Slovenia, with lots of vintage sellers from the states like Philly’s Betsu and Chicago’s Spears Furnishings selling their wares on Etsy as well.

eBay brought me such things as this vintage Tarogo frog made from Ichiban rice paper that I passed up in a thrift store in Maine and thought about for months before it surfaced on the secondhand retailer. Now he sits proudly on an armoire overlooking my dining room. Which is to say: Every vintage table lamp that’s ever existed is somewhere in their backlog. Chinoiserie, vintage Noguchi lamps, kitschy conch shell lamps, Tiffany glass shades, the OG Pixar lamp—it’s all there.

Design Within Reach regularly re-issues iconic models in collaboration with the original manufacturers, giving second life to pieces like Verner Panton’s Panthella (1971), Herman Miller’s 1952 Cigar Lotus floor lamp, Greta Grossman’s 1947 Gräshoppa, and the Space Age-y Nessino table lamp which debuted in 1967, to name a few.

Rejuvenation’s vintage collection is part of a larger initiative to prevent waste. The brand’s Portland-based restoration studio team finds and restores over 3,000 antiques around the world every year to help keep them out of landfills. While the vintage pieces are one-of-a-kind finds, a large selection mirrors Rejuvenation’s midcentury modern-inspired offerings, like 20th-century brass lamps and designs with floral and gilt detailing.

Abask has some of the most beautiful antique Murano glassware lamps we’ve seen to date. Case in point: Albano Poli’s stained glass creation pictured below. The artist got his claim to fame for collaging colored glass across geometric lighting fixtures. Modern glass lamps like this one are easy to come by across Abask’s collections, as well as minimalist metal lamps and hand-painted ceramic lamps, if those better suit your style.

#4919. Probing the Depths of a Drive-by

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

"Imagination is more important than knowledge"—Albert Einstein

Imagination has an assortment of meanings and often works in different and perplexing ways.

Merriam-Webster defines imagination as “the act or power of forming a mental image of something not present to the senses or never before wholly perceived in reality."

So imagine the term “drive-by.” It has an assortment of definitions. One of the more established is an assault where a perpetrator fires a weapon from a moving vehicle, then flees the scene.

“Drive-by” is also the name of a celebrated rock band—the Drive-By Truckers.

But the most relevant connotation to me, sadly, is when one pretends to care about a person in need or a highly emotive issue, then quickly moves on for various reasons. Among them: Perhaps they simply don’t understand or are overwhelmed by the circumstances; they can’t embrace emotional trauma or disease; or they’re shallow individuals caught up with self-aggrandizement; or they flat-out don’t really care about the health or well-being of others.

Words like callous and self-centered come to mind.

So, they often punt, in words that have no inner meaning.

I find this true in my journey with Alzheimer’s and an advancing prostate and chest cancer diagnosis—diseases embedded in my family. I’m one of millions.

The gut response often tends to be: “But you look so good!”

The truth here is that Alzheimer’s and cancer don’t affect, at the start, how one looks. It’s the inner core of the diseases that torments. And so, in their great uneasiness about discussing the specifics, many punt.

I’ve pondered this over time, working hard not to feel irritated about it. Seems to me, there’s a proclivity these days for many to be absorbed with self. We see it in advertising; we see it in movies; we see it in social conversations about the size of one’s home, investments, money in the bank, or worldly accomplishments and possessions.

With such individuals, a common response to those in need is to espouse in a drive-by at best: “I’m here for you!”

Well, what the heck does that mean? Unless one embraces the need or at least wants to be educated about it, the response comes across as shallow as low tide on Cape Cod Bay, which runs out to the horizon for miles,

Writes Archie James: “The people who don’t really care about you are so difficult to identify. They are present. They are warm enough. They are soft enough on the surface. They say the right words. They are not cold. They say anything like: ‘That’s amazing' and 'I’m so proud of you!’

“On the surface,” adds James, “if you would describe this conversation to someone else, it might sound like support. It would pass the test. But something doesn’t land. You hang up the phone—or leave the room—and you feel vaguely emptier than you did before.”

Many say the perception today that people in general have become more superficial is driven perhaps by advancing technologies, shifts in culture, addiction to social media, or simply checking out from the whirlwind of modern life. We collectively absorb a 24/7 news cycle of wars, world crises, staggering suffering, and crushing violence. And so many of us suffer at times from compassion fatigue, and race to hit the pause button—a numbing defense mechanism worldwide.

Pump the brakes on this. I now realize that I’m in the driver’s seat at times as well—neglecting the needs of others. Research is enlightening.

Commenting on a worldwide scale, Paul Slovic, an academic expert in human judgment, says that many people are generally caring “and will exert great effort to rescue individual victims whose needy plight comes to their attention. These same good people, however, often become numbly indifferent to the plight of individuals who are one of many in a much greater problem.”

Says the Arithmetic of Compassion: “Psychic numbing is a psychological phenomenon that causes us to feel indifferent to the suffering of large numbers of people. The quote attributed to Joseph Stalin—‘One death is a tragedy; a million deaths is a statistic’—is an illustration of psychic numbing.”

Notes Bessel van der Kolk, a Dutch American psychiatrist and researcher, in his book, The Body Keeps the Score: “Traumatized people (worldwide) chronically feel unsafe inside their bodies. The past is alive in the form of gnawing interior discomfort. Their bodies are constantly bombarded by visceral warning signs, and, in an attempt to control these processes, they often become expert at ignoring their gut feelings and at numbing awareness of what is played out inside. They learn to hide from themselves.”

Author Jessica Sorrensen had it right when she reflected, “I just let the pain take over, allowing it to numb the pain of being left behind.”

And observed Bethany Griffin, author of Masque of the Red Death, “I’ve perfected the art of the fake smile. It’s not so difficult when you are completely numb.”

The fake smile… mea culpa... We’ve all used it.

And so, many caring individuals have become somewhat detached these days, and in many ways for understandable reasons.

So, how do we know what others really feel deep inside? That’s often a crapshoot in these days of political correctness, keeping to party lines, not baring the soul in reflective ways.

Perhaps with oxygen tanks. Perhaps not, for now.

Thus, one needs to use imagination to climb out of a box that people place you in when they say they want to help; they want to sympathize, but they don’t.

Fully noted: As an Irish Catholic, I’m thinking now that I need to be back in the confessional on this.

One often needs imagination, I’ve learned the hard way, to walk in knowledge—for knowledge is limited and imagination is vast, as Einstein notes.

Even more so on the lip of holiday times.

Griffin, B. (2012). Masque of the Red Death. Greenwillow Books.

Merriam-Webster Dictionary. Imagination. Retrieved from: https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/imagination

#4910. Using AI to Avoid Thinking Harms Students

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Kaja Perina

The conclusion of this blog post is so important for students that I want to start with it:

If you are learning something that makes you think, using AI to avoid thinking is a misuse. AI use is appropriate when it prompts you to think more or to help you accomplish “busy work,” which requires little thinking.

In light of this statement, helpful uses of AI in education include:

Students may suffer when their use of AI reduces or eliminates their need to wrestle with a problem. This impairs learning, because:

I asked seven consecutive adolescent patients who have come to my counseling practice how they have been using AI to help with their schoolwork. Unfortunately, I believe each one of them reported a potentially harmful misuse, which they did not even realize.

As we review these misuses, it should be kept in mind that major goals of education should not be attaining good grades or correct answers, but rather acquiring knowledge and how to better understand and generalize it.

A high school sophomore was given an assignment to take notes about his history reading, and then to summarize what he learned in three sentences. He dutifully read the material and typed his notes into an AI Chatbot. He then asked AI to summarize the notes in three sentences, which he turned in.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Taking notes is an insufficient tool for learning (especially when the notes are typed rather than handwritten). Rather, deciding which is the most salient information from the notes to put into a summary is the activity that best promotes learning from this assignment.

A high school senior was dealing with a difficult homework problem in her math class. She asked an AI to show her how to solve the problem. The AI showed her the step-by-step solution. After she felt she understood the explanation, she went on to study her other subjects.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Just because this student understood the AI-generated explanation did not mean that she could utilize this explanation in solving further problems. She should have worked through a few other similar problems without help of the AI to ensure that she understood how to apply the underlying principles (Bastani et al., 2025).

Another high school senior who was taking several advanced placement classes used AI to summarize the highlights of books he was supposed to read for English class. He then wrote essays for this class using the AI-generated material.

Missed Learning Opportunity: How to extract essential information from reading material is a learned skill. While it is tempting to use AI for this purpose, a human reader may find different salient information by reading an original source. For instance, an AI summary may fail to comment regarding how an author presented detailed subject matter intended to evoke a reader’s emotions.

A high school junior asked AI to compose e-mails to his teachers about missed assignments and potential make-up work.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Students should learn how adding a human element as part of a written communication is more likely to generate favorable response. For instance, I quickly delete emailed queries from students requesting the opportunity to work with me if they appear to be AI-generated.

A high school sophomore told me he has used AI to verify the news he has heard on social media.

Missed Learning Opportunity: Given generative AI’s propensities to hallucinate and echo what it has been told (sycophancy) using AI to verify the news is a poor practice (Fletcher & Verckist, 2025). Instead, this student should learn how to use primary sources to verify news, such as consulting reports by a few news organizations.

The last two examples of potential misuse were prompted by teachers rather than the students:

An 8th grader was told by his science teacher to use AI to make a poster that presents what he had learned about a particular topic.

Missed Learning Opportunity: While I appreciate the teacher’s desire to teach students how to apply AI in their lives, in 8th grade it might be much more important for students to learn how to apply the elements that make for an effective poster presentation. For instance, how to decide on an appropriate title, choose the effective top line summaries, and what information should be included while maintaining readability of the poster. As part of this process, students also would learn how to prioritize the information they gathered.

A 9th grader was given an assignment by his English teacher to define different words, identify their part of speech, and to provide their language of origin. The student completed the assignment without consulting AI, and was downgraded because he didn’t give the exact definition of the word as listed by an AI. Furthermore, the student was aware that his teacher used an AI to grade the assignment.

Missed Learning Opportunity: According to the student in this example, his teacher is enthusiastic about using AI, and teaching students how to do so. Unfortunately, his teacher’s whole-hearted adoption of AI is pushing the student to forego his independent thinking and learning process in favor of allowing AI to shape his work.

Students may be tempted to use AI as a short-cut to complete their assigned work. However, as demonstrated in this blog, learning can be greatly diminished by using AI.

Students’ use of AI to prompt their thinking is good. Their use of AI to avoid thinking is detrimental. Thus, when students face difficulty in understanding an assignment, they should ask for hints from their instructors or an AI, rather than answers.

Bastani, H., et al. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(26), Article e2422633122.

Dunlosky, J., et al. (2013). Improving students’ learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

Fletcher, J., & Verckist, D. (2025, October). News integrity in AI assistants: An international PSM study. European Broadcasting Union & British Broadcasting Corporation.

Kestin, G., et al. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: An RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports, 15, Article 17458.

#4901. How to Meditate to Help Reduce Shame

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Meditation is a tool for creating distance between yourself and the onslaught of default thoughts, emotions, and sensations that make up our moment-to-moment experiences. This distance enables choice and provides the most profound type of personal freedom on offer: the freedom to decide how you feel about things, your sexuality being chief among them.

Here is the most basic meditation I’m aware of. Try it if you dare:

You don’t need to spend a ton of time practicing to reap significant benefits. I recommend starting with ten to fifteen minutes a day, three days a week. But even as little as a couple of minutes a week can make a difference.

The benefits of meditation have become so sensationalized by the self-help industry that it’s important to be clear about what its actual purpose is. Meditation will not produce startling insights into the mysteries of the universe. Your IQ and personality will remain unchanged. If you suck at pickleball before meditating, you will suck afterward. But do it enough—starting with a few minutes a few times a week—and you will notice that your mind has become a little less frantic, a little less hooked by doom loops, and a little more spacious.

Meditation is a way to create space between us and our unproductive thoughts, and it can therefore offer relief from shame. Try doing a meditation practice when you feel yourself getting into a negative mindset. When you experience that stench of shame associated with your fetish, notice it as a thought arising out of nowhere. You did not ask for that feeling of shame, and it in no way helps you. Let it go and bring your attention to your breath. It will probably arise again—notice that, and again gently but firmly return your attention to your breath. There is no need for you to react to or add commentary to your shame—don’t pile new thoughts onto the shame thought and don’t recoil from it—just notice it and bring your attention back to the breath.

This is not about avoiding unpleasant thoughts; it is simply about recognizing and not elaborating on them. Shame is just a thought arising in your mind like any other thought, and it is in its nature to pass away (thanks, Buddha). Simply processing your shame thoughts in this way will eventually strip them of their emotional power. So much of our suffering is the result of obsessive elaboration on the things that pop into our heads. Somatic exercises are meant to help us stop piling on.

Allow me to introduce an analogy based on my beloved New York City, whose sidewalks burst with every type of human imaginable, all of whom jump into your field of vision all the time. You can’t control who walks by or what might be on the sidewalk. They simply appear. You might notice the pretty girl, the cold-eyed businessman, the kindly older man helping his wife across the street, or the guy you think is waiting to pick your pocket. Your thoughts are the same. Simply notice them when they pop up next to you on the sidewalk.

Let’s walk through a common shame spiral I see in my work: Imagine you’re scrolling Instagram on the couch. Someone has posted a fashion photo of a person wearing latex. There’s a brief moment of excitement, followed immediately by, "This is so shallow. Why can’t I be turned on by something normal?" That thought brings in the others: "This is weird. I shouldn’t be turned on by this. How can I possibly live a normal life with this desire?" Now your attention is no longer on the image itself—it’s on the story you’re telling about your desire.

From there, the thoughts intensify. You start replaying past rejections—that time you brought a date to the sex toy store, and they judged you for wanting them to try on latex, etc. Within seconds, a neutral moment of arousal has turned into a full-on spiral.

Notice what’s happening here. The fetish didn’t create the suffering. The thought about the fetish did. This is where the sidewalk metaphor becomes useful. You didn’t choose who walked by, but you stopped, stared, followed, and built based on what you saw. A meditation-trained mind might instead note, "Arousal happened," or "That person looks hot in latex," just as it might note, "That smells bad," and then keep moving. The practice isn’t to pretend the sidewalk is empty. It’s to stop writing poems about the pile of sh*t.

Excerpted from my book, Fetish: Smash Taboos and Celebrate What Turns You On.

#4898. Construction Carnaval: electric equipment comes to Brazil with SDLG

SDLG Brasil has completed its first sale in the South American country, delivering an order of six heavy-duty electric wheel loaders to Brazilian mining, construction, and infrastructure company Grupo Base.

Grupo Base ordered four, 27-ton L972 HEV and a pair of, 12.5-ton L938 HEV loaders from Chinese equipment brand Shandong Lingong Construction Machinery Co., Ltd. (the “SD” is “ShanDong,” the LG is “LinGong”) back in June, and the first of the machines are now reportedly on-site, moving dirt, but not making noise.

“This contract is a historic milestone and comes at a time when we have taken on commercial responsibility for SDLG across 60% of Brazil,” says Carlos Renato Machado, executive director of SDLG’s Brazilian distributor, Tracbel, before adding that the company hoped to expand the use of electric mining and construction equipment throughout the region.

The SDLG machines draw power from 423 and 180 kWh LFP battery packs, respectively, with the larger machines sending power to a 230 kW (~305 hp) electric motor and the smaller machines getting a 180 kW (~240 hp) one. Both specs promise a full day’s worth of continuous operation and fast DC charging between shifts.

Grupo Base operates a fleet of 450 heavy equipment assets at more than 30 concrete and mortar batching plants and 20 crushed stone and fracking sand sites, employing more 2,000 people. The electrification of those assets would represent a massive environmental benefit to the ecologically sensitive region – and that’s a fact not lost on Grupo Base executives.

“We are driving a major transformation across our operations,” says Edson Pechio, president and CEO of Grupo Base, said. “We want to incorporate solutions that will enable us to operate more efficiently and progressively reduce greenhouse gas emissions.”

#4896. Volkswagen recalls nearly 73,000 EVs due to faulty batteries

Volkswagen issued a recall affecting nearly 73,000 EVs globally. Until a remedy is available, VW will limit charging on impacted vehicles to 80% of their maximum battery capacity.

After issuing a recall with the NHTSA earlier this month that impacts 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs in the US, official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) reveals several thousand more EVs are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, a total of 72,668 EVs are impacted worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

Volkswagen issued the recall after an internal investigation found that some battery cells produced during that period do not meet specifications. The recall stems from a supplier defect.

In some instances, “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation,” or a battery fire, Volkswagen said.

Until a remedy is available, Volkswagen is urging owners to limit charging to 80% of its max capacity. If technically possible, VW said: “the maximum available charging capacity will be temporarily limited to 80% by the system.”

In the US, Volkswagen emailed owners of vehicles included in the recall, saying that unless they opt out by October 21, it “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%.”

The update will be done remotely and reflected in the mobile app on or about October 27, 2026. Some owners have already received the update.

Sounds like VW's "GM Bolt" moment. Sad. This is a huge cost due to a supplier's failure (but fully understandable and needed), not to mention owners frustration with EVs and the brand.

Volkswagen is still working on a remedy. Letters informing owners of the risks are expected to be mailed out on November 27, 2026. Once the remedy is available, VW will send additional letters.

Owners can contact Volkswagen’s customer service at 1-800-893-5298 with questions or concerns. VW’s recall number is 93EX.

Those in the US can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Vehicle Safety Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit NHTSA.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V630.

The manufacturer’s recall codes with the German KBA are 93MV, 93MF, and 93W4 (for the Cupra Born).

#4895. Have You Ever Had Sex That Felt Scary?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 2, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In 2014, the White House Task Force to Protect Students from Sexual Assault found that 20 percent of college women get raped as undergraduates. The report generated controversy. That many? Really? The controversy spurred research. Three years later, a large study by investigators at many U.S. colleges and universities concluded the statistic was “reasonably accurate.” (Muehlenhard, 2017)

During the decade since that Task Force, many colleges, universities, and the military have instituted rape-prevention programs that inform young women of their risk, warn against getting drunk at parties, and encourage “designated sober” bystanders to intervene if they see trouble. Those programs have reduced women’s risk of sexual assault in higher education and the military by 50 percent.

Rape-prevention programs have also spotlighted the fact that some problematic young-adult sexual interactions don’t constitute sexual assault, but are still unwanted and scary. Recently, Indiana University researchers investigated who experiences scary sex and why.

The researchers surveyed 721 undergraduates, average age 19, at Indiana University, 49 percent women, 49 percent men, 2 percent other, divided roughly evenly among first-, second-, third-, and fourth-year students. Almost 80 percent were heterosexual, with 12 percent bisexual, 5 percent lesbian/gay, and 4 percent transgender or gender non-binary. Half were single, half in relationships. Completing the 20-minute survey entered them in a lottery for $100 gift cards. (Herbenick, 2025)

Almost one-third of survey respondents (31 percent) reported at least one sexual experience they called scary. Three-quarters of them (75 percent) were women, 21 percent were men, and 5 percent were transgender or gender non-binary.

The researchers grouped scary experiences into seven categories:

This is not the only study to delve into frightening sex. Two pilot reports by Indiana University researchers showed that 25 percent of women and 10 percent of men reported sometimes feeling scared during sex. (Herbenick, 2019, 2022) Those studies inspired this larger one.

Scary sex may include activities that are standard elements of bondage-discipline-sado-masochism (BDSM): restraint, rough play, and sacrifice of control. But in mutually pleasurable BDSM, the players negotiate their play beforehand. They agree to every move, and everyone knows exactly how the play will unfold. They also adopt “safe words” to stop the action if anyone feels uncomfortable or scared.

Across all categories, some participants of every gender and sexual preference reported feeling scared. But overwhelmingly, they were women and sexual and gender minorities—and their fear was inspired by male partners. In other words, the problem is out-of-control young men. Parents, older siblings, college staff, and mental health professionals should tell young men repeatedly and bluntly that they better control themselves or they risk prison.

What makes men lose control? Usually alcohol. Although today’s young adults drink less than previous generations, alcohol continues to fuel reckless behavior. Anyone who deals with young people should tell them repeatedly and bluntly that alcohol intoxication may embroil them in situations they would rather avoid. Beer commercials say “drink responsibly.” To prevent scary sex, a better message would be “just one drink if any, no more.”

Young adults experiment with both sex and drugs. We’ve all been there and know that some of those experiments play with fire. To avoid getting burned, young adults should take responsibility for their safety by:

Some might call this victim-blaming. It’s not. It’s taking adult responsibility for personal safety. That’s prudent—and as this study shows, unfortunately necessary.

Herbenick, D et al. “‘I Just Really Didn’t Know What I Was Walking Into,’: Scary Sexual Experiences in a Campus-Representative Survey of Undergraduate Students,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2025) 51:58. Doi: 10.1080/0092623X.2024.2433102.

Herbenick, D et al. “‘It Was Scary, But Then It Was Kind of Exciting’: Young Women’s Experiences with Choking During Sex,” Archives of Sexual Behavior (2022) 51:1103. Doi: 10.1007/s10508-021-02049-x.

Herbenick, D et al. “Feeling Scared During Sex: Findings from a U.S. Probability Sample of Women and Men Ages 14 to 60,” Journal of Sex and Marital Therapy (2019) 45:424. Doi: 10.1080/0092623x.2018.1549634.

Kilimnik, CD, et al. “Undergraduate Students’ Definitions of Sexual Violence Labels Across the Rise of the #MeToo Movement,” Psychology of Women Quarterly (2024) 48:430. Doi: 10.1177/03616843241239634.

Klein, LB, et al. “Sexual and Relationship Violence Among LGBTQ+ College Students: A Scoping Review,” Trauma, Violence, and Abuse (2023) 24:2196. Doi: 10.1177/15248380221089981.

Muehlenhard, CL et al. “Evaluating the One-In-Five Statistic: Women’s Risk of Sexual Assault While in College,” Journal of Sex Research (2017) 54:549. Doi: 10.1080/00224499.2017.1295014.

#4894. The Surprising Ways Professional Dancers Overcome Performance Anxiety—and How to Do It Yourself

These science-backed strategies will help you enter a calmer state.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As the audience settles in their seats and the orchestra begins tuning its instruments, Isabella Boylston, 40, is hit with a sense of panic backstage. Even after 20 years of performing in front of audiences, the American Ballet Theatre principal dancer isn’t immune to performance anxiety. “I feel like a tiny furnace of adrenaline is burning inside of me, my brain is working overtime going through steps and scenarios, and I also feel like I get less circulation to my fingers and toes,” she says.

Whether you’re giving a presentation during a meeting, training for a race, or even getting ready for a date, performance anxiety is extremely common. In fact, 63 percent of the general population reports experiencing anxiety around public speaking. “Performance anxiety can show up in any sort of activity that involves being evaluated or where there is some expectation of the level you’re trying to perform at,” says sport and counseling psychologist Natalie Léger, PsyD. Worry and doubt about the outcome are “extremely normal,” she says. But despite how commonplace anxiety is around performance, it can be hard to manage, and even harder to talk about.

Dancers are no strangers to performing under high-stress situations—and oftentimes, performing through less-than-ideal circumstances such as injury, illness, or minimal rehearsal time. That’s especially true right now, as professional ballerinas gear up for one of their busiest seasons of the year, when they perform The Nutcracker for the holidays. That’s why we turned to some of the pros for their best tips to help regain control over nerves. Here’s what they recommend.

“The first step in being able to tackle anxiety is awareness,” says American Ballet Theatre director of repertoire Nancy Raffa, who helps teach the dancers choreography and mental health practices, and holds a degree in psychology. “Anxiety is a built-up fear towards an outcome that hasn’t happened yet, so instead of criticizing yourself that there’s something wrong with you, ask yourself what it is that you’re anxious about to start shifting the thought process.” Then, give yourself grace and know that how you feel is totally valid.

It's in these moments that Léger suggests introducing some short affirmations, reminding yourself that you’re capable and prepared. You can also try instructional self-talk, which helps shift your attention to the present by giving yourself a small assignment to focus on like holding your shoulders back and your head high. “Our emotion center of the brain is really activated within moments like this, and so if you give yourself instruction, that starts to bring oxygen to the part of the brain that’s more related to decision-making and thinking logically,” she says.

You can’t always predict when anxiety will creep in, but having a well-structured routine can give you a sense of security ahead of that anxiety-inducing activity, says Léger. Jasmine Perry, 31, a corps de ballet dancer with Miami City Ballet, focuses on the root of her anxiety, which is the fear that fatigue will interfere with her performance ability. “So, I focus on what makes me feel strong,” she says. Perry prioritizes getting at least seven hours of sleep, eating balanced meals, and making sure that anything she needs for performance day is ready to go the night before.

Sleep CheckInsufficient sleep can make anxiety worse. If you struggle to go to sleep the night(s) before a big talk or performance, develop a routine around sleep. That may look like “staying away from the screens in the hour leading up to sleep, not working out too close to going to sleep, ensuring that your bed is not a place that you’re reading or watching TV,” Léger says.

A growing amount of research points to a correlation between increased social media use and anxiety. So, consider assessing your social media habits to take stock of where your “energy is being pulled or supported,” says Léger. “For example, feeling checked out while doomscrolling when trying to go to sleep is highly unlikely to support optimal performance, while watching a video of a chef make a recipe you’re interested in trying after training can feel like it’s supporting your creative mind, which can be helpful for performance.”

Start by limiting your screen time around your sleep schedule, both before you go to bed at night and when you wake up in the morning, Léger says. Training yourself to resist reaching for your phone as soon as you wake up helps to put you in touch with the present moment, which is the goal ahead of a performance.

During the busiest seasons, Boylston often completely deletes her social media apps. “It helps me feel more focused and there’s less temptation to self-sabotage and compare myself with others,” she says. Can’t commit to a full social media detox? Perry recommends using an app like Opal to limit your use, or you can use the app time limit setting on your phone to set up timers for specific apps.

The night before or in the hours leading up to a stressful task, Perry finds a quiet, calm environment and takes a few minutes to herself. “I try to visualize the thing that I have to do, and in that image in my mind, implement the things I need to consider the next time that I do it,” she shares. “That way, I’ve had time to think, and process, and let it all settle in, so I’m able to allow those things to happen more naturally, versus physically trying to go over everything in the moment in a panic.”

The key to an effective visualization practice is to make the scene you’re envisioning feel as real as possible, says Léger. Ahead of a presentation, that might mean picturing the room you’ll be speaking in, as well as your audience, or even trying on the outfit you plan to wear. “All of these elements, felt through your own eyes, can lead to the brain firing the same neurons it would in a real-life performance, just at a lesser intensity,” she explains. This practice can also boost confidence by making the task feel more familiar.

Breathing from your diaphragm signals a relaxation response in the body and brings the heart rate back down. “If you think about it, if you were actually under threat, you would never slow down to take a deep breath, you would just act quickly,” says Léger. “Through deep breathing, you’re starting to introduce to your nervous system, ‘I’m okay, I’m safe.’”

Try alternate nostril breathing, says Raffa. Inhale through your left nostril as you hold the right side closed, then switch to exhale through the right nostril as you hold the left side closed (and alternate as you repeat the exercise). Or try deep belly breaths: “Put one hand on your chest and one hand on your lower abdomen and do five to 10 deep breaths where you inhale and let the belly expand out, then exhale and let the belly go back in,” she says. If it helps, breathe with a rhythm by doing three counts in, three counts out.

In the hours (and even days) leading up to a stressful task, it can be hard to stop yourself from obsessing over the unknown. That’s when it’s time to change focus and soothe your brain. “I try to do something that’s totally unconnected to what I have to do that evening, whether it’s reading a book or getting outside and looking at nature,” says New York City principal dancer Emma Von Enck, 29. She also has her own playlist of classical music that calms her down—almost like white noise—before she gets ready for a show.

If you feel like your anxiety is more severe or interfering with your day-to-day life, Léger recommends getting in touch with a mental health professional. But leaning on your family, close friends, or a trusted colleague is also key. “When you talk with peers and articulate what your experience might be, a lot of people are going to see how so much of this is just a normal part of the human experience,” she adds. Normalizing performance anxiety and knowing that you’re not alone goes a long way in helping to ease some of the burden.

It may also be comforting to read up on performance anxiety. Boylston recommends The Inner Game of Tennis by W. Timothy Gallwey, which helped her learn how to stay present and not fixate on the outcome of a situation. Or, try Peak Performance by Brad Stulberg and Steve Magness, which examines the practices of top performers across the arts, sports, and business. Von Enck credits it with helping her to hone her own pre-performance routine.

At some point, though, do your best to let go of control. “In anything where you’re trying to excel, you want to control every element, but you have to be flexible in seeing it as a challenge when something isn’t going perfectly,” Von Enck says. And know that it might take some time to master the art of performance anxiety. “Getting to a place where you can quiet the mind is a process,” says Raffa. “It’s just like dancing; to master the technique, you need to repeat, repeat, repeat.”

Meet the experts: Natalie Léger, PsyD, is a sport and counseling psychologist, mental performance consultant, and the owner of The Collective Edge, a sports and counseling psychology private practice in Washington, D.C. Isabella Boylston is a principal dancer with American Ballet Theatre in New York City. Nancy Raffa is the American Ballet Theatre director of repertoire who helps teach the dancers choreography and mental health practices, and holds a degree in psychology. Emma Von Enck is a principal dancer with New York City Ballet. Jasmine Perry is a corps de ballet dancer with Miami City Ballet.
